title: Closing carbon balances when weathering cations are retained
open: Separate atmospheric CO₂ consumption from strong-acid weathering, ion exchange and secondary-mineral storage over complete wet–dry cycles.
status: A 2025 replicated hillslope study closed carbon and water balances and exposed gas-diffusion and incongruent-dissolution limits. Transferable agricultural-soil verification remains open.
why: Prevents missing or released cations from being equated directly with permanent removal.
key_works: C. J. Cunningham et al. (2025), *Carbon dioxide removal during dissolution of granular basalt: A mass balance test of enhanced rock weathering at the hillslope scale*, [DOI:10.1016/j.epsl.2025.119662](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.epsl.2025.119662).

title: Preventing delayed Cr(VI) rebound after reductive remediation
open: Predict and prevent Cr(VI) regeneration as Cr–Fe hydroxides age toward goethite in the presence of manganese, oxygen and changing pH.
status: A 2025 study found approximately tenfold higher Cr(VI) release following mineral transformation under its conditions. Long-term control across residue compositions remains open.
why: Ensures reduced chromium residues remain immobilized during aging.
key_works: S. Xie et al. (2025), *Enhanced oxidation of Cr(III) with the mineral transformation of CrxFe1-x(OH)3 in the presence of Mn(II): overlooked process during the reoccurrence of Cr(VI) in reduced chromite ore processing residue*, [DOI:10.1016/j.envpol.2025.126327](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envpol.2025.126327).

title: Atomic conversion pathway from proto-C-S-H to binding hydrate
open: Resolve the rearrangement of disordered calcium–silicate precursors into C-S-H and predict induction times from solution chemistry, surfaces and additives.
status: A 2025 scattering study found predominantly six-coordinate calcium in proto-C-S-H versus seven-coordinate calcium in the product, with gluconate prolonging precursor persistence. The full pathway remains open.
why: Connects cement setting to identifiable molecular events.
key_works: R. Besselink et al. (2025), *High energy X-ray scattering reveals the short-range order of proto-C-S-H: Implications for the nucleation of cement hydrates*, [DOI:10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107855](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107855).

title: Aluminium-dependent lifetime of prenucleation cement globules
open: Predict how aluminium concentration and coordination govern amorphous C-A-S-H globule persistence and conversion across blended-cement pore solutions.
status: A 2025 study established a two-step pathway at Ca/Al = 5 and increased persistence with aluminium. Composition-wide kinetic prediction remains open.
why: Connects low-clinker composition to workability and setting.
key_works: Y. H. Emminger, L. Ladner and C. Ruiz-Agudo (2025), *Comparative study of the early stages of crystallization of calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H) and calcium aluminate silicate hydrate (C-A-S-H)*, [DOI:10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107873](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107873).

title: Decoupling cement dispersion from hydrate-nucleation retardation
open: Design dispersants lowering water demand without unwanted setting delays, predicting separate effects on dissolution, hydrate nucleation and portlandite precipitation near saturation.
status: Four polymers inhibited hydrate nucleation without measurable dissolution inhibition under tested undersaturation in 2025. Near-saturation and mixed-clinker behavior remain unresolved.
why: Preserves early strength while reducing mixing water.
key_works: A. Vohburger et al. (2025), *Influence of Polymeric Dispersants on the Dissolution Rate of Tricalcium Silicate and the Nucleation of Calcium-Silicate-Hydrate and Portlandite*, [DOI:10.1002/chem.202500207](https://doi.org/10.1002/chem.202500207).

title: Distinguishing dissolution-driven and rearrangement-driven cement creep
open: Separate stress-assisted dissolution/reprecipitation, hydrate sliding and continuing hydration contributions to creep, predicting their humidity and composition dependence.
status: The microscopic origin remains debated. A 2025 study found continued fly-ash reaction increasing creep and foil-like C-A-S-H in slag blends inhibiting it; quantitative mechanism separation remains open.
why: Links hydrate chemistry to long-term structural deformation.
key_works: J. Wang et al. (2025), *Does the hydration process of supplementary cementitious materials affect the aging creep of blended cement paste?*, [DOI:10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107826](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107826).

title: Transferable reactivity assay for compositionally variable cement substitutes
open: Predict unfamiliar supplementary materials’ reaction extent and strength contribution from standardized chemical and structural measurements.
status: A July 2026 comparison of 18 materials used modified R3 testing and thermodynamic normalization, finding seven-day reactivity indices of 2–55%. Broad prospective validation remains open.
why: Enables reliable use of local clays, slags, ashes and residues.
key_works: B. K. Aylas-Paredes et al. (2026), *Bridging Composition, Structure, and Reactivity to Performance in a Wide Range of Supplementary Cementitious Materials*, [DOI:10.1111/jace.71034](https://doi.org/10.1111/jace.71034).

title: Carboaluminate acceleration without sacrificing later binder stability
open: Control carbonate dissolution and aluminate availability to accelerate low-clinker hardening while preserving stable hydrate assemblages across variable wastes and sulfate levels.
status: A 2026 carbonated-waste/calcined-clay system accelerated carboaluminate chemistry. Transferable phase and kinetic control across heterogeneous feeds remains unresolved.
why: Addresses slow early strength without increasing clinker content.
key_works: X. Du et al. (2026), *Development of Carbonated Waste-Enhanced Calcined Clay Cement (CWC3) via Activated Carboaluminate Reaction: A Strategy toward Sustainable Engineering Materials*, [DOI:10.1021/acssuschemeng.5c11743](https://doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.5c11743).

title: Predicting steel passivity after alkali-activated binder carbonation
open: Predict steel depassivation from evolving pore solutions and hydrates during carbonation, chloride exposure and leaching.
status: A 2025 calcined-clay/slag study observed no corrosion after the carbonation front reached steel, consistent with retained high pH. Conventional front criteria therefore lack universal transferability.
why: Provides chemically valid durability criteria for alternative binders.
key_works: S. D. C. Gomes et al. (2025), *Shrinkage and carbonation of alkali-activated calcined clay-ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBFS) concrete*, [DOI:10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107899](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107899).

title: Chemical predictor of alkali–silica expansion after decades outdoors
open: Predict expansion from ASR-product chemistry, alkali supply and hydration history, distinguishing damaging products from similar nonexpansive deposits.
status: ASR has been studied since the twentieth century. A 2026 analysis of specimens exposed since 1992 adds rare long-term evidence; transferable prediction remains open.
why: Connects accelerated assessments to actual infrastructure aging.
key_works: M. Ranger, A. Leemann and B. Fournier (2026), *An ASR exposure site after 30 years – Chemical composition of hydrates and ASR products*, [DOI:10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.108043](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.108043).

title: Pore-specific ettringite nucleation thresholds for delayed cracking
open: Predict which pores nucleate delayed ettringite and develop damaging pressure from supersaturation, confinement and sulfate release.
status: A 2025 SAXS study followed four cements for up to 4,000 days and inferred a 20–25 nm critical range. General composition- and history-dependent thresholds remain open.
why: Enables prevention of delayed expansion in heat-cured concrete.
key_works: M. S. Islam, Y. Shekar and B. J. Mohr (2025), *Nanoscale pore structure analysis of cementitious materials subjected to delayed ettringite formation*, [DOI:10.1016/j.cement.2025.100145](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cement.2025.100145).

title: Bypassing self-passivation during low-temperature MgO carbonation
open: Sustain MgO carbonation in humid low-CO₂ environments by controlling product-layer growth without repeated high-energy milling or layer removal.
status: A 2025 single-crystal study observed rapid initial reaction followed by slowing hydroxide/carbonate growth. Preventing practical-particle passivation remains open.
why: Improves carbonating binders and mineral sorbents.
key_works: P. Yang et al. (2025), *Carbonation of MgO Single Crystals: Implications for Direct Air Capture of CO2*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.est.4c09713](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.4c09713).

title: Pair-specific RO₂ accretion branching beyond small radicals
open: Measure absolute reaction constants and accretion yields for unlike multifunctional peroxy-radical pairs, testing whether self-reaction rules predict cross-reactions.
status: A 2025 small-β-hydroxy-RO₂ study measured accretion-channel constants spanning approximately \(4.7\times10^{-13}\) to \(8.0\times10^{-16}\) cm³ molecule⁻¹ s⁻¹. Complex atmospheric radicals remain inadequately covered.
why: Controls low-volatility product formation and particle growth.
key_works: S. E. Murphy et al. (2025), *Accretion product formation in the self- and cross-reactions of small β-hydroxy peroxy radicals*, [DOI:10.1039/D5EA00106D](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5EA00106D).

title: Surface accretion of RO₂ on freshly nucleated particles
open: Directly test peroxy-radical accretion at sulfuric-acid/base nanoparticle interfaces, measuring competition with desorption and gas-phase reaction.
status: A 2026 computational study identified rapid candidate pathways. Particle-size-resolved experimental confirmation and atmospheric-flux relevance remain missing.
why: Could explain organic growth immediately after particle nucleation.
key_works: G. Hasan, T. Kurtén, I. Neefjes and J. Elm (2026), *Can Accretion Products Be Formed at the Interface of Freshly Nucleated Particles?*, [DOI:10.1021/acsomega.5c13316](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.5c13316).

title: Ambient importance of peroxide–nitrite organic-nitrate formation
open: Quantify organic-nitrate production from peroxide–nitrite reactions in real particles, resolving precursor structures, acidity and water content.
status: Three commercial peroxides produced roughly 13–15% organic-nitrate yields at pH 3 in 2025 experiments. The pathway’s ambient contribution remains unmeasured.
why: Changes reactive-nitrogen sequestration and particle-nitrogen budgets.
key_works: Y. Yang et al. (2025), *Multiphase reactions of organic peroxides and nitrite as a source of atmospheric organic nitrates*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-60696-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-60696-3).

title: Isomer-resolved organic-nitrate hydrolysis in concentrated aerosol
open: Measure individual monoterpene-nitrate hydrolysis and competing reactions in low-water-activity aerosol across acidity, ionic strength and organic matrices.
status: Seven synthesized standards studied in 2021 showed strongly structure-dependent minute-to-hour lifetimes, with some secondary nitrates resistant under neutral conditions. Actual aerosol matrices remain insufficiently characterized.
why: Determines whether aerosol nitrates recycle atmospheric nitrogen oxides.
key_works: Y. Wang et al. (2021), *Synthesis and Hydrolysis of Atmospherically Relevant Monoterpene-Derived Organic Nitrates*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.est.1c05310](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.1c05310).

title: Origin of unequal nitrate-aerosol yields from the two phellandrenes
open: Identify particle-phase pathways explaining α-/β-phellandrene nitrate-oxidation yield differences, closing carbon and nitrate balances with resolved products.
status: A 2025 chamber study found maximum aerosol yields near 35% and 60%, respectively, despite similarities in measured gas chemistry. The condensed-phase explanation remains incomplete.
why: Tests how terpene structure should enter regional aerosol models.
key_works: S. Harb et al. (2025), *Highly oxygenated molecules (HOMs) and secondary organic aerosol (SOA) formation from the oxidation of α- and β-phellandrenes by NO3 radicals*, [DOI:10.5194/acp-25-11003-2025](https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-25-11003-2025).

title: Direct ambient speciation of larger stabilized Criegee intermediates
open: Measure larger stabilized Criegee intermediates and their conformers selectively at ambient concentrations without creating them during measurement.
status: Direct CH₂OO detection from ethene ozonolysis was demonstrated in 2025. Species-resolved measurement of larger intermediates in real air remains open.
why: Directly tests their modeled oxidation and particle-formation roles.
key_works: M. Campos-Pineda, L. Yang and J. Zhang (2025), *Direct measurement of the Criegee intermediate CH2OO in ozonolysis of ethene*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-61739-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-61739-5).

title: Experimental test of four-acid iodine–sulfur nucleation synergy
open: Measure rates and cluster compositions for sulfuric, methanesulfonic, iodic and iodous acid mixtures, isolating each component’s contribution under marine conditions.
status: A 2025 quantum-chemical/kinetic study predicted enhancement reaching seven orders of magnitude under selected modeled conditions. The four-component mechanism requires experimental validation.
why: Tests a potential source of otherwise unexplained marine particles.
key_works: R. Zhang et al. (2025), *Quaternary Nucleation of Iodine and Sulfur Oxoacids in the Marine Atmosphere: Unexpected Role of Methanesulfonic Acid*, [DOI:10.1029/2024JD042220](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024JD042220).

title: Reactive-solute control of aqueous HPMTF sulfur branching
open: Determine whether realistic cloud solutes alter hydroperoxymethyl thioformate reaction mechanisms and branching, with closed sulfur and carbon balances.
status: A 2024 experiment already found sulfate consistent with unit yield and carbonyl sulfide below 1.2%; 2025 field observations confirmed substantial cloud removal. Solute-dependent chemistry remains unresolved.
why: Connects marine DMS oxidation to sulfate and carbonyl-sulfide budgets.
key_works: C. M. Jernigan et al. (2024), *Sulfate and Carbonyl Sulfide Production in Aqueous Reactions of Hydroperoxymethyl Thioformate*, [DOI:10.1021/acsestair.3c00098](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsestair.3c00098); D. B. Kilgour et al. (2025), *Cloud processing of dimethyl sulfide (DMS) oxidation products limits sulfur dioxide (SO2) and carbonyl sulfide (OCS) production in the eastern North Atlantic marine boundary layer*, [DOI:10.5194/acp-25-1931-2025](https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-25-1931-2025).

title: Road-salt-dependent inland nitryl-chloride source inventory
open: Quantify N₂O₅ uptake and ClNO₂ yields on aged road-salt aerosol, resolving coatings, mixed salts and humidity for inland winter inventories.
status: Fresh salts tested in 2026 gave uptake coefficients around 0.003–0.067 and yields from undetected to near unity. Their regional aged-particle importance remains unestablished.
why: Quantifies an inland photolabile chlorine source.
key_works: J. A. Christie, K. A. Pratt and C. J. Gaston (2026), *Road-Salt Aerosol Reacts More Efficiently with N2O5 than Sea Spray Aerosol to Produce ClNO2*, [DOI:10.1021/acsearthspacechem.6c00042](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsearthspacechem.6c00042).

title: Chemical origin of nitryl chloride emitted during automotive braking
open: Identify chloride sources and reaction sequences generating braking-associated ClNO₂, separating new tribochemistry from release of existing material.
status: HONO, ClNO₂ and N₂O₅ were detected during braking in 2025. Precursor inventories and a closed nitryl-chloride production mechanism remain unresolved.
why: Reveals reactive gas emissions omitted by particle-mass inventories.
key_works: M. E. Cooke et al. (2025), *Emissions of Nitrous Acid, Nitryl Chloride, and Dinitrogen Pentoxide Associated with Automotive Braking*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.est.4c13202](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.4c13202).

title: Identity of the mid-polarity Pacific iron-binding ligand group
open: Isolate unidentified mid-polarity iron-binding compounds from the Pacific GP15 transect and determine structures, affinities and degradation pathways.
status: A 2025 survey found unresolved putative siderophores in upper-mesopelagic tropical waters. Coelution prevented confident molecular-ion and formula assignments.
why: Converts a recurrent oceanographic signal into an interpretable transport mechanism.
key_works: J. Li, L. Babcock-Adams, M. R. McIlvin and D. J. Repeta (2025), *Distribution and Cycling of Siderophores in the Eastern North and Tropical Pacific Oceans*, [DOI:10.1029/2024GL113874](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GL113874).

title: Seawater siderophore dissociation constants that predict microbial iron access
open: Measure representative ferric-siderophore dissociation kinetics in seawater and distinguish dissociation-limited microbial access from receptor-mediated uptake.
status: A 2026 study found contrasting enterobactin/ferrichrome bioavailability to SAR11 and other heterotrophs. Seawater kinetic constants cover too few ligands for general prediction.
why: Binding strength alone may misidentify biologically accessible iron.
key_works: D. L. McRose, C. Völker and F. M. M. Morel (2026), *Contrasting bioavailability of enterobactin- and ferrichrome-bound iron to SAR11 and other marine heterotrophs*, [DOI:10.1093/ismeco/ycag113](https://doi.org/10.1093/ismeco/ycag113).

title: Chemical structures of Arctic copper-binding dissolved organic molecules
open: Determine native Arctic Cu-ligand structures and coordination sites, connecting each to a measured binding constant.
status: A 2025 separation/HRMS study assigned 511 formulas in Cu-binding fractions. Complete structures and binding geometries remain unresolved.
why: Explains copper availability and toxicity in changing Arctic waters.
key_works: L. Criqui and C. Guéguen (2025), *Advancing the characterization of organic Cu(II)-binding ligands in Arctic Ocean waters: Integration of IMAC, SPE, HRMS, and fluorescence techniques*, [DOI:10.1016/j.marchem.2025.104578](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marchem.2025.104578).

title: Recovery-corrected census of native marine copper ligands
open: Correct native Cu-ligand inventories for weak complexes lost or transformed during affinity chromatography and extraction.
status: The 2025 Arctic study found only 7–25% overlap between molecular peaks from alternative workflows. Method selection obstructs reconstruction of original seawater distributions.
why: Prevents extraction biases from masquerading as geographic variation.
key_works: L. Criqui and C. Guéguen (2025), *Advancing the characterization of organic Cu(II)-binding ligands in Arctic Ocean waters: Integration of IMAC, SPE, HRMS, and fluorescence techniques*, [DOI:10.1016/j.marchem.2025.104578](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marchem.2025.104578).

title: Identity of non-cobalamin cobalt-binding ligands in the surface ocean
open: Identify strong cobalt ligands not accounted for by measurable cobalamins, including oxidation states and biological sources.
status: A 2025 North Pacific study measured approximately 31–87 pM dissolved cobalt without detecting cobalamin-related compounds in the corresponding strong-ligand pool. Remaining ligand structures are unknown.
why: Explains stabilization and exchange of scarce marine cobalt.
key_works: J. Park et al. (2025), *Efficient cobalamin uptake and cycling contribute to the lack of cobalamins in the surface cobalt-binding ligand pool in the North Pacific*, [DOI:10.1002/lol2.70019](https://doi.org/10.1002/lol2.70019).

title: In situ pathway accounting for oceanic dimethylmercury formation
open: Quantify biological methylation and abiotic reduced-sulfur contributions at natural concentrations, identifying reactive complexes and pathway-specific rates.
status: A 2025 incubation/observation/modeling study reproduced aspects of marine methylmercury distributions, but assumptions about dimethylmercury persistence prevented unique formation-pathway attribution.
why: Identifies sources feeding the oceanic methylmercury cycle.
key_works: A. Kleindienst et al. (2025), *Incubation Experiments, Observations, and Modeling Highlight the Key Role of Dimethylmercury on Seawater Methylmercury Distributions*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.est.5c01491](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.5c01491).

title: Mechanisms converting dimethylmercury into monomethylmercury at depth
open: Identify and measure dimethylmercury conversion pathways below strongly illuminated surface waters independently of concentration-profile fitting.
status: A 2024 upwelling study inferred net loss of \(2.0\pm1.1\%\) per day from field profiles and mass-budget modeling. Direct pathway-specific field rates remain unresolved.
why: Explains methylmercury production away from immediate primary formation sites.
key_works: H. M. Adams, X. Cui, C. H. Lamborg and A. T. Schartup (2024), *Dimethylmercury as a Source of Monomethylmercury in a Highly Productive Upwelling System*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.est.4c01112](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.4c01112).

title: Partitioning photochemical and microbial sources of oceanic elemental mercury
open: Measure gross photochemical and microbial Hg(0) production separately, resolving native ligands, Hg(I) intermediates and back-oxidation.
status: A 2025 North Pacific study found inefficient net photoreduction; 2026 experiments revealed strong ligand and inorganic-carbon effects. Transferable source partition remains open.
why: Determines whether deposited mercury remains oceanic or returns to the atmosphere.
key_works: L. C. Motta, J. D. Blum and B. N. Popp (2025), *Photoreduction of Inorganic Mercury in Surface Seawater*, [DOI:10.1021/acsearthspacechem.5c00219](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsearthspacechem.5c00219); S. Eom et al. (2026), *Mechanistic Insights into Mercury Photoreduction: Effects of Dissolved Organic Matter and Inorganic Carbon in Seawater*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.est.5c15961](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.5c15961).

title: Chemical evolution and self-limiting growth of ZDDP tribofilms
open: Predict coupled phosphate-chain chemistry, film growth and removal under changing stresses, identifying the chemical feedbacks limiting thickness.
status: A 2023 study separated shear-promoted growth from compression-induced inhibition. A complete growth–conversion–removal network for service contacts remains missing.
why: Maintains wear protection with lower additive consumption.
key_works: L. Fang et al. (2023), *What stress components drive mechanochemistry? A study of ZDDP tribofilm formation*, [DOI:10.1039/D2FD00123C](https://doi.org/10.1039/D2FD00123C).

title: Experimental kinetic law for electrically assisted phosphate-ester tribochemistry
open: Measure reaction rates and product distributions jointly against field, shear and temperature, testing predicted reversals between weak- and strong-field effects.
status: A 2025 nonequilibrium simulation predicted nonmonotonic field dependence. A chemically resolved, experimentally calibrated law spanning these regimes remains open.
why: Explains lubricant changes in electrically stressed machinery.
key_works: Z. Zhu and J. P. Ewen (2025), *Mechanochemistry of phosphate esters with external electric fields*, [DOI:10.1039/D5MR00064E](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5MR00064E).

title: Selecting protective MoS₂ pathways during MoDTC decomposition
open: Predict branching among MoS₂, oxysulfides and oxides as water, oxygen, surfaces and co-additives change, linking products to sustained wear protection.
status: TiO₂ nano-additives altered MoDTC-film evolution and improved lubrication in a 2025 study. Transferable product-selection rules remain unresolved.
why: Avoids formulations that provide only transient low friction.
key_works: Z. Fan et al. (2025), *Synergetic lubrication between MoDTC and TiO2 nano-additive: Dynamic evolution of tribofilm induced by tribocatalysis and tribomechanical effect*, [DOI:10.1016/j.triboint.2025.110608](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.triboint.2025.110608).

title: Predicting PFPE molecular lifetime in heat-assisted recording contacts
open: Translate PFPE scission mechanisms on diamond-like carbon into validated lifetimes under realistic thermal pulses and contact loads, resolving end-group and surface effects.
status: Reactive simulations in 2025 identified shear-sensitive, end-group-dependent degradation. Their short timescales and idealized contacts do not establish service lifetimes.
why: Lubricant failure limits increasingly hot and compact recording interfaces.
key_works: H. Shekhar et al. (2025), *ReaxFF molecular dynamics study of mechanochemical degradation of PFPE lubricants on DLC in heat-assisted magnetic recording*, [DOI:10.1039/D5MR00023H](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5MR00023H).

title: Retaining chemically generated superlubricity through environmental cycling
open: Maintain friction below 0.01 with low wear during repeated temperature, humidity and load changes, identifying stable interfacial chemistry and regeneration pathways.
status: SiOₓ-stabilized graphitization produced friction near 0.002 at 300 °C in air in 2026. Reproducible durability across changing service conditions remains open.
why: Converts exceptional laboratory friction into reliable component performance.
key_works: J. Chen et al. (2026), *Stable high-temperature superlubricity enabled by thermomechanical-induced interfacial graphitization and SiOx-mediated structural locking*, [DOI:10.1039/D5MH02175H](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5MH02175H).

title: Native structure of soluble methane monooxygenase intermediate Q
open: Establish Q’s Fe–O connectivity, protonation and Fe–Fe distance while reconciling vibrational, X-ray and magnetic spectra for the same intermediate population.
status: Debated for over 30 years. A 2021 QM/MM study favors an open core; complete experimental discrimination from diamond-core assignments remains unresolved.
why: Identifies how a biological diiron center activates methane.
key_works: C. E. Schulz et al. (2021), *Structure–Spectroscopy Correlations for Intermediate Q of Soluble Methane Monooxygenase: Insights from QM/MM Calculations*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.1c01180](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c01180).

title: Alternating-site turnover in soluble methane monooxygenase
open: Determine whether hydroxylase halves obligatorily alternate turnovers, measuring coupling among MMOB binding, oxygen activation and product release.
status: A 2026 2.85 Å structure with one MMOB reveals asymmetric approximately 2.7/3.1 Å diiron separations. Structural asymmetry does not establish kinetic alternation.
why: Explains protein-scale control of oxidant formation.
key_works: Y. Hwang et al. (2026), *Cryo-EM Structures Reveal the Molecular Basis of Asymmetric Allosteric Activation by MMOB in the Hydroxylase of Soluble Methane Monooxygenase*, [DOI:10.1002/advs.202517312](https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.202517312).

title: Catalytic role of nitrogenase’s interstitial carbide
open: Determine how carbide bonding changes across turnover states and whether those changes causally enable substrate binding or hydrogen transfer.
status: Carbide identity is established. A 2026 analysis reconciles geometric rigidity with variable σ/π bonding; state-resolved tests of catalytic function remain open.
why: Explains the function of an unusual carbon-centered metal cluster.
key_works: J. P. Joyce and S. DeBeer (2026), *Recasting Nitrogenase’s Carbide Role as a Beating Heart of Steel: A Joint Inorganic and Organic Perspective for μ6Carbide–Iron Bonding*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c05356](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c05356).

title: Atom-by-atom molybdenum insertion into the nitrogenase precursor
open: Resolve apical iron removal, molybdenum insertion and homocitrate attachment during L-cluster conversion, accounting for expelled iron, electrons and ATP.
status: The 2026 NifX-to-NifEN structures resolve precursor trafficking, but the inferred internal conversion site and metal-exchange chemistry remain uncaptured.
why: Makes complex cofactor assembly more reproducible outside native hosts.
key_works: F. F. Schneider et al. (2026), *Trafficking of a nitrogenase FeMo-cofactor assembly intermediate*, [DOI:10.1038/s41589-026-02179-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41589-026-02179-0).

title: Substrate coordination in catalytically active methyl-coenzyme M reductase
open: Determine methyl-SCoM coordination in active Ni(I) enzyme through C–S cleavage, discriminating nickel–sulfonate binding from sulfur-coordinated alternatives.
status: A 2021 study supports nickel–sulfonate binding; 2025 atomic structures add constraints. A native active-state substrate-to-radical trajectory remains missing.
why: Establishes the geometry enabling methane formation and its reversal.
key_works: A. Patwardhan et al. (2021), *Nickel–Sulfonate Mode of Substrate Binding for Forward and Reverse Reactions of Methyl-SCoM Reductase Suggest a Radical Mechanism Involving Long-Range Electron Transfer*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.1c01086](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c01086); M.-C. Müller et al. (2025), [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-63387-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63387-1).

title: ATP-to-redox coupling in methyl-coenzyme M reductase activation
open: Measure ATP consumption per Ni(II)-to-Ni(I) activation, identify the physiological donor and resolve the gate preventing futile ATP cycling.
status: A 2025 activation-complex structure and ATP-dependent reactivation with an artificial reductant reveal a plausible three-cluster electron route. Physiological stoichiometry and gating remain unresolved.
why: Removes a barrier to reliable heterologous methane metabolism.
key_works: F. Ramírez-Amador et al. (2025), *Structure of the ATP-driven methyl-coenzyme M reductase activation complex*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-08890-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-08890-7).

title: Functions of the unusual modifications in methane-oxidizing MCR
open: Assign individual post-translational modifications’ causal effects on methane activation, cofactor stability and directionality through controlled modification states and kinetics.
status: Atomic-resolution ANME-2c/2d structures identified extensive modifications in 2025. Their individual chemical functions remain unassigned.
why: Identifies maturation functions required when transferring methane-oxidation machinery.
key_works: M.-C. Müller et al. (2025), *Atomic resolution structures of the methane-activating enzyme in anaerobic methanotrophy reveal extensive post-translational modifications*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-63387-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63387-1).

title: Native nickel–methyl–carbonyl intermediate in acetyl-CoA synthase
open: Detect and assign the native intermediate bearing methyl and CO before C–C formation, or establish a mechanism bypassing an observable intermediate.
status: A synthetic nickel methyl–carbonyl species was characterized in 2025. Native spectroscopy in 2026 supports one CO in the ambient reduced carbonyl state, but does not identify the mixed precursor.
why: Identifies the immediate precursor to biological acetyl-group formation.
key_works: S. Nath, L. Griego and L. M. Mirica (2025), *The mechanism of acetyl-CoA synthase through the lens of a nickel model system*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-60163-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-60163-z); D. Poire et al. (2026), *From two to one: resolving CO binding in acetyl-CoA synthase*, [DOI:10.1039/D5SC08875E](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5SC08875E).

title: Electron accounting during ACS thioester release
open: Determine whether native acetyl-CoA release uses oxidation-triggered nickel chemistry, tracking the transferred electron through enzyme reset.
status: One-electron oxidation accelerated thioester elimination approximately 1,800-fold in a 2025 model. The corresponding native oxidation sequence remains unverified.
why: Discriminates mechanisms with different electron-donor and cofactor requirements.
key_works: S. Nath, L. Griego and L. M. Mirica (2025), *The mechanism of acetyl-CoA synthase through the lens of a nickel model system*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-60163-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-60163-z).

title: Flux through alternative ACS substrate-binding orders
open: Quantify CO-first versus methyl-first turnover and its dependence on domain motion and concentrations, distinguishing productive routes from trapped states.
status: Six ACS/CODH states were captured at 2.5–1.9 Å in 2025. Structural feasibility does not determine kinetic flux through competing orders.
why: Explains substrate inhibition and operating constraints in biological CO fixation.
key_works: J. Ruickoldt et al. (2025), *Ligand binding to a Ni–Fe cluster orchestrates conformational changes of the CO-dehydrogenase–acetyl-CoA synthase complex*, [DOI:10.1038/s41929-025-01365-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-025-01365-y).

title: Suppression of short circuits at the Bfu flavobicluster
open: Establish the FMN/Fe–S redox sequence coupling favorable and unfavorable electron transfer in NfnABC, quantitatively explaining suppression of favorable-branch leakage.
status: Structures identified an FMN–[4Fe–4S]–[2Fe–2S] minimum bifurcation unit in 2025. A directly tested mechanism with measured leakage rates remains open.
why: Reveals how low-potential chemistry can be driven without ATP.
key_works: H. Li et al. (2025), *Cryo-EM reveals a composite flavobicluster electron bifurcation site in the Bfu family member NfnABC*, [DOI:10.1038/s42003-025-07706-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-025-07706-8).

title: Direct observation of proton sharing during NiFe-hydrogenase turnover
open: Measure proton localization and exchange between conserved cysteine and glutamate within native Ni-L and Ni-R populations, including second-sphere gating.
status: A 2026 multiscale model reproduces important spectra through proton sharing. Direct time-resolved confirmation of populations and gating rates remains open.
why: Connects hydrogenase spectra to catalytic proton-transfer dynamics.
key_works: S. Moorthy, G. Joshi and A. Sirohiwal (2026), *Dynamic Proton Sharing and Second-Sphere Gating Control Catalytic States in [NiFe] Hydrogenase*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.6c05074](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.6c05074).

title: Identity of the mitochondrial sulfur cargo for cytosolic Fe–S assembly
open: Identify the sulfur-containing ABCB7/Atm1 cargo supporting cytosolic Fe–S assembly, including its iron content and ligands, then reconstitute export-to-target incorporation.
status: The X-S intermediate remains unassigned after decades of evidence. The 2026 ABCB7 heme-export structures establish additional cargo chemistry without identifying X-S.
why: Connects mitochondrial chemistry to cytosolic and nuclear enzyme maturation.
key_works: S. Ju et al. (2026), *Cryo-EM structures of human ABCB7 reveal the molecular basis of mitochondrial matrix heme export*, [DOI:10.1038/s42003-026-10223-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-026-10223-x); R. Lill laboratory, [Biosynthesis of cellular iron–sulfur proteins and the impact on cellular iron homeostasis](https://www.uni-marburg.de/en/fb20/departments/cyto/group/prof-lill/biosynthesis-of-cellular-iron-sulfur-proteins-and-the-impact-on-cellular-iron-homeostasis).

title: Secure detection of interstellar glycine
open: Identify interstellar glycine through multiple unblended transitions with consistent excitation and abundance, no missing strong lines and explicit conformer discrimination.
status: The disputed early-2000s claim never became secure. A September 2026 preprint still treats interstellar glycine as undetected and examines conformer kinetics as a search constraint.
why: Anchors links between interstellar chemistry and planetary amino-acid inventories.
key_works: L. E. Snyder et al. (2005), *A Rigorous Attempt to Verify Interstellar Glycine*, [NIST record](https://www.nist.gov/publications/rigorous-attempt-verify-interstellar-glycine); J. Wurmel and J. M. Simmie (2026), *Glycine in the interstellar medium revisited: Resolving conformational complexity kinetically*, [arXiv:2609.17243](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17243).

title: Carrier of the 6614 Å diffuse interstellar band
open: Identify a molecule reproducing the band’s laboratory wavelength, substructure and environmental profile changes, with viable interstellar formation and survival.
status: Unassigned. A 2025 oblate-top fit suggests roughly 54 carbon atoms under that model; competing geometric interpretations remain possible.
why: Identifies a major molecular population hidden from rotational surveys.
key_works: C. Bhatt et al. (2025), *The EDIBLES Survey IX: Simulations of the λ6614 DIB Profile Variations: A Surprising Connection with CH⁺*, [DOI:10.1021/acsearthspacechem.4c00238](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsearthspacechem.4c00238); H. MacIsaac et al. (2022), [DOI:10.1051/0004-6361/202142225](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202142225).

title: Small-molecule hypothesis for the 6196 Å DIB family
open: Identify the 6196 Å carrier and determine whether correlated side bands belong to one small linear molecule, ion or weakly bound complex.
status: A 2025 EDIBLES analysis found correlated side features supporting a small-carrier interpretation. Contour fits have not produced a definitive assignment.
why: Tests whether prominent DIBs can arise from unexpectedly small species.
key_works: A. Ebenbichler et al. (2025), *The EDIBLES survey: X. The 6196 Å diffuse interstellar band: Identification of side DIBs as an indication of a small carrier molecule*, [DOI:10.1051/0004-6361/202453259](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202453259); [arXiv:2502.06386](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06386).

title: Carrier and charge state of the 8621 Å diffuse interstellar band
open: Assign the 862.1 nm band to a molecule and charge state using laboratory spectra and a consistent photoionization/recombination model.
status: A 2026 study of 12 clouds finds spatial behavior supporting a cation. Ionization-energy constraints remain model-dependent and do not identify the molecule.
why: Gives Gaia’s extensive DIB measurements a chemical identity.
key_works: H. Zhao and L. Li (2026), *A cationic carrier for the diffuse interstellar band at 862.1 nm: Evidence of the skin effect in nearby diffuse to translucent clouds*, [DOI:10.1051/0004-6361/202557833](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202557833); [arXiv:2603.05631](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05631).

title: Carrier of the 6379 Å diffuse interstellar band
open: Identify the absorber while explaining rotational substructure and excitation changes, breaking the degeneracy between linear and approximately spherical geometries.
status: A 2022 contour analysis yields geometry-dependent rotational constants; the spherical interpretation implies roughly 77–114 carbons. No molecular formula is securely assigned.
why: Distinguishes chemical families with similar astronomical band profiles.
key_works: H. MacIsaac et al. (2022), *The EDIBLES survey V: Line profile variations in the λλ5797, 6379, and 6614 diffuse interstellar bands as a tool to constrain carrier sizes*, [DOI:10.1051/0004-6361/202142225](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202142225); [arXiv:2203.01803](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01803).

title: State-resolved energy partition in grain-mediated H₂ formation
open: Measure and predict nascent H₂ rotational, vibrational and translational distributions on realistic amorphous grains, including energy retained by the surface.
status: A 2025 ab initio study resolves dissipation on graphene-based models. Transferable experimental distributions across realistic grain structures remain unavailable.
why: Controls gas heating, emission and subsequent H₂ chemistry.
key_works: L. Jubert et al. (2025), *Energy partitioning in H₂ formation on interstellar carbonaceous grains. Insights from ab initio molecular dynamics simulations*, [DOI:10.1039/D5CP01585E](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5CP01585E).

title: Site-resolved ortho–para conversion of adsorbed hydrogen
open: Measure distributions of rotational-energy splitting, conversion rates and residence times on heterogeneous grains, then predict gas-phase H₂ spin ratios.
status: A 2026 model relaxes the assumption that adsorption preserves the gas-phase 170.5 K splitting. Results remain sensitive to incompletely measured surface quantities.
why: Improves cold-cloud chemical clocks and deuteration predictions.
key_works: K. Furuya et al. (2026), *H₂ Ortho–Para Spin Conversion on Inhomogeneous Grain Surfaces. II. Impact of the Rotational Energy Difference between Adsorbed Ortho-H₂ and Para-H₂ and Implication for Deuterium Fractionation Chemistry*, [DOI:10.3847/1538-4357/ae43e3](https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/ae43e3); [arXiv:2602.13122](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13122).

title: Chemical memory of concurrent irradiation and ice warm-up
open: Predict products for defined ices under specified overlapping UV-flux and temperature histories, validating dose-rate effects on held-out histories.
status: Experiments in 2026 compare simultaneous and sequential irradiation/warm-up with flux and fluence controls. Extrapolation to slow astronomical histories remains open.
why: Makes laboratory ice chemistry quantitatively usable in planet-formation models.
key_works: C. C. Sarver, C. E. Walker and S. L. Widicus Weaver (2026), *Laboratory Investigation of Simultaneous Ultraviolet Photoprocessing and Temperature-Programmed Desorption of Interstellar Ice Analogs*, [DOI:10.1021/acsearthspacechem.5c00338](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsearthspacechem.5c00338).

title: Interstellar abundance and survival of glycylglycine
open: Identify glycylglycine unambiguously in interstellar gas or ice and explain its abundance through formation, destruction, heating and grain-release kinetics.
status: Proton-driven formation in cryogenic glycine analogues was demonstrated in 2026. This establishes a laboratory route without an integrated astrophysical yield or interstellar detection.
why: Tests whether peptide bonds can precede planet formation.
key_works: A. T. Hopkinson et al. (2026), *An interstellar energetic and non-aqueous pathway to peptide formation*, [DOI:10.1038/s41550-025-02765-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-025-02765-7).

title: Joint nitrogen, carbon and hydrogen isotope closure in PDS 70
open: Reproduce resolved HCN/HC¹⁵N, HCN/H¹³CN and DCN/HCN profiles with one chemistry–transport model, distinguishing self-shielding, exchange chemistry and excitation bias.
status: A 2025 study found the nitrogen ratio declining outside the approximately 50 au cavity wall while carbon and deuterium behaved differently. Selective N₂ photodissociation is suggested but not uniquely established.
why: Connects observed isotope ratios to material accreted by planets.
key_works: L. Rampinelli et al. (2025), *Radial variations in the nitrogen, carbon, and hydrogen fractionation in the PDS 70 planet-hosting disk*, [DOI:10.1051/0004-6361/202554172](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202554172); [arXiv:2504.03833](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03833).

title: Post-impact chemical memory in the solid-state Finkelstein reaction
open: Identify the activated species or interfacial state that allows halogen exchange to continue after milling stops, and measure its formation and decay independently of cumulative mechanical energy.
status: Templ and Borchardt separated impact, aging and liquid-assisted effects in 2026. Their Finkelstein reaction showed pronounced post-milling conversion, whereas the comparison Wittig reaction tracked cumulative energy much more closely.
why: Makes interrupted milling and storage history predictable reaction variables.
key_works: J. Templ and L. Borchardt (2026), *Experimental Isolation of Single Impact, Cumulative Energy, Aging, and Liquid-Assisted Grinding Effects in Mechanochemical Reactions*, [DOI:10.1002/anie.202523191](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202523191).

title: Motif-II structure of the hydrated electron in water clusters
open: Assign the atomic structure and electron-binding geometry of motif II in size-selected water-cluster anions. A convincing assignment must explain photoelectron and absorption measurements obtained under the same source conditions.
status: An and Kim’s 2026 measurements expanded the experimentally distinguished motifs from four to five; the correspondence between motif II and calculated structures remains unresolved.
why: A secure assignment would test how a small hydrogen-bond network stabilizes an excess electron.
key_works: S. An and S. K. Kim (2026), “Structure and isomer-specific femtosecond real-time relaxation dynamics of hydrated electron motifs in water cluster anions,” [DOI: 10.1038/s42004-026-02006-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-026-02006-6).

title: Water evaporation versus electron loss in the 340-ps cluster-anion decay
open: Resolve the branching between neutral-water evaporation and electron autodetachment from vibrationally excited water-cluster anions, including its dependence on cluster size and electron-binding motif.
status: An and Kim (2026) observed an approximately 340-ps ground-state decay component and provisionally attributed it to evaporation and/or autodetachment; channel-specific identification remains open.
why: Establishes how small hydrated electrons survive after optical excitation.
key_works: S. An and S. K. Kim (2026), “Structure and isomer-specific femtosecond real-time relaxation dynamics of hydrated electron motifs in water cluster anions,” [DOI: 10.1038/s42004-026-02006-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-026-02006-6).

title: Funding sustained real-seawater validation of novel membrane chemistry
open: Fund continuous, independent pilot testing that exposes new membrane materials to representative seawater, cleaning cycles, and chemical aging, producing evidence usable in procurement decisions.
status: XPRIZE’s May 2026 report identifies funding constraints among 130 teams and pilot-access constraints among 71; it separately identifies long-duration validation and manufacturing barriers for materials teams.
why: Promising laboratory chemistry needs operating evidence before utilities can assess replacement materials.
key_works: H. Atoufi/XPRIZE Foundation (2026), “Innovation Landscape Report: XPRIZE Water Scarcity,” [official report](https://www.xprize.org/news/innovation-landscape-report-xprize-water-scarcity).

title: First identified optical transitions of neutral lawrencium
open: Observe and assign a neutral-lawrencium optical transition, then use the level structure to test predicted relativistic valence configurations.
status: The 2026 search scanned approximately 800 cm⁻¹ around each of two predicted strong transitions without detecting either. The experiment demonstrated efficient evaporation and sufficient sensitivity, leaving the transition locations or excitation assumptions unresolved.
why: Supplies direct electronic-level evidence for the final actinide.
key_works: E. Rickert et al. (2026), “Progress toward identifying atomic transitions in lawrencium,” [DOI: 10.1140/epjd/s10053-026-01198-9](https://doi.org/10.1140/epjd/s10053-026-01198-9).

title: Identity and causal role of the m/z 259.12891 pinking marker
open: Identify the unassigned mass-spectrometric feature associated with Muscat pinking and Roditis skin contact, then determine whether it is a chromophore, precursor, or correlated product.
status: A June 2026 conference poster reported signal increases of 576% in pinked Muscat and 1,977% in the fourfold-skin-contact Roditis treatment. Its structure and causal contribution to color remain unassigned.
why: Provides a specific molecular target for understanding unpredictable wine pinking.
key_works: P. Gimenez-Gil, C. Virgiliou, and G. Theodoridis (2026), “Characterisation of pinking precursors in Muscat and their dose-dependent accumulation in a Roditis skin-contact model,” [WAC–IVAS poster abstract](https://ives-openscience.eu/64494/).

title: Unknown side products that divert irradiated chromium recombination
open: Identify the accumulating products that cause Cr(I)/Cr(III) recombination in molten LiCl–KCl to depart from second-order kinetics, and determine their reaction pathways.
status: Pulse-radiolysis measurements resolved primary reactions, but increasing accumulated dose introduced competing chemistry whose products remained unidentified.
why: Reveals when reversible radiation chemistry produces persistent changes in a molten salt.
key_works: K. Iwamatsu et al. (2026; first published 2025), “Kinetics of radiation-induced Cr(II) and Cr(III) redox chemistry in molten LiCl–KCl eutectic,” [DOI: 10.1039/D4CP04190A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4CP04190A).

title: Radium-223 chelation that survives tracer-level dilution in serum
open: Produce a molecular Ra(II) chelate that remains intact after dilution into serum, distinguishing intact complex from free radium in every analytical fraction. Demonstrate stability over the intended delivery interval without excess free ligand recapturing dissociated radium.
status: A 2026 screen achieved quantitative room-temperature labeling with 14 of 17 chelators, but even macropa dissociated within one hour at higher dilution. Apparently favorable size-exclusion results could conceal free radium.
why: Enables targeted radium delivery beyond its natural bone-seeking behavior.
key_works: J. W. Southwell, M. Gumiela et al. (2026), “Synthesis, Characterization, and Evaluation of Chelators for Radium-223,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c04877](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c04877).

title: Molecular identity of physiological astatine colloids
open: Establish the oxidation state, composition, and bonding of retained astatine species formed in physiological media. Distinguish an astatine oxyhydroxide phase from protein-associated or mixed colloids.
status: A 2026 study detected oxidation-associated non-anionic fractions and ultrafilter-retained material. Its AtOOH assignment rests on a proposed thermodynamic interpretation rather than direct structural identification.
why: Connects organ retention of released astatine to an identifiable chemical species.
key_works: X. Dong et al. (2026), “Redox-driven speciation and colloid formation contribute the in vivo chemistry and organ deposition of Astatine-211,” [DOI: 10.1186/s41181-026-00441-3](https://doi.org/10.1186/s41181-026-00441-3).

title: Experimental hydration-state exchange of aqueous Ac–DOTA
open: Measure populations and exchange rates of Ac–DOTA configurations containing one versus two inner-sphere water molecules. Test whether water exchange accompanies transient opening of DOTA donor arms.
status: A 2026 hybrid ML/MM model predicts approximately 37.5% one-water and 59.9% two-water configurations and picosecond exchange. Experimental population and kinetic measurements remain a proposed validation target.
why: Supplies actinium coordination dynamics needed to evaluate chelate-dissociation mechanisms.
key_works: J. Vant, S. Khan, V. Ngo, D. Bykov, and D. Bhowmik (2026), “Actinium–DOTA coordination in water from hybrid ML/MM: Structure, free energies, and water-exchange pathways,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.aichem.2026.100125](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aichem.2026.100125).

title: Does a transient cyclic astatinane protect ortho-substituted aryl–At bonds?
open: Detect or exclude the proposed intramolecular arylalkoxyastatinane formed when a neighboring benzyl-alcohol group encounters oxidized aryl astatine. Quantify its contribution to suppressed C–At cleavage.
status: Ortho alcohols improved resistance to chemical and microsomal oxidation in 2025. The hypothesized cyclic intermediate could not be observed, and steric shielding alone did not explain the chemical-oxidation results.
why: Turns an effective stabilization motif into a transferable radiolabel-design mechanism.
key_works: R. Fouinneteau, C. Maingueneau, N. Galland, C. Perrio, and F. Guérard (2025), “Ortho-functionalization of a 211At-labeled aryl compound provides stabilization of the C-At bond against oxidative dehalogenation,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41598-025-01162-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-01162-4).

title: Unidentified cleavage products of lead–TCMC thiourea bioconjugates
open: Identify the radioactive metabolites and serum components that detach targeting vectors from Pb–TCMC thiourea conjugates. Distinguish linker cleavage from radiometal loss.
status: A 2025/2026 study found similar degradation products for FAPI and CycMSH conjugates; amide replacements improved stability. Attempts to identify products using nonradioactive lead and LC–MS encountered sensitivity limits, leaving their identities and formation mechanisms unresolved.
why: Prevents intact metal chelation from being mistaken for an intact targeting molecule.
key_works: B. L. McNeil et al. (2026; online 2025), “Is Thiourea the Weak Link? An Investigation of the In Vitro and In Vivo Destabilization of [203Pb]- and [212Pb]Pb2+ Thiourea-Based Bioconjugates,” [DOI: 10.1021/acsbiomedchemau.5c00224](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsbiomedchemau.5c00224).

title: Competitive-ligand boundary for loss of protactinium’s mono-oxo bond
open: Determine the composition-dependent boundary between mono-oxo and non-oxo Pa(V) complexes in mixed chloride/fluoride and other competing acidic media. Measure species fractions across that boundary.
status: A 2026 study established a roughly 1.83 Å Pa–O bond persisting even in highly acidic chloride solution. Its persistence with competing ligands remains unresolved; acidity alone does not provide the missing speciation rule.
why: Makes protactinium chemistry predictable across changes of medium.
key_works: M. Maloubier et al. (2026; online 2025), “Persistent Mono-Oxo Bonding with Protactinium(V) Revealed in Highly Acidic Chloride Solutions,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.202518403](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202518403).

title: Resolving inverse trans influence in a Pa(V) solution complex
open: Experimentally distinguish trans and cis Pa–Cl distances in the mono-oxo chloride complex. Test the predicted inverse trans influence independently of fitting a calculated geometry.
status: The 2026 analysis predicts trans-bond shortening of 0.04–0.08 Å. That difference falls within the EXAFS uncertainty and was not resolved experimentally.
why: Tests a directional-bonding prediction for an exceptionally data-poor actinide.
key_works: M. Maloubier et al. (2026; online 2025), “Persistent Mono-Oxo Bonding with Protactinium(V) Revealed in Highly Acidic Chloride Solutions,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.202518403](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202518403).

title: Ligand-dependent origin of einsteinium’s blue-shifted luminescence
open: Predict and measure how donor atoms and coordination geometry shift Es(III) emission. Separate changes in spin–orbit mixing from ligand-field and vibronic contributions.
status: The 2021 Es–HOPO study observed a hypsochromic shift unlike earlier lighter-actinide complexation examples and proposed intermediate coupling with strong j–j character. A quantitatively tested ligand-series explanation remains a proposed extension.
why: Establishes whether optical trends from lighter actinides remain predictive near the series end.
key_works: K. P. Carter et al. (2021), “Structural and spectroscopic characterization of an einsteinium complex,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-03179-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-03179-3).

title: Room-temperature Pr(V) persistence beyond the demonstrated protective ligand environment
open: Isolate a room-temperature-persistent molecular Pr(V) complex beyond the demonstrated heavily shielded imidophosphorane environment. Measure decomposition kinetics and establish its electronic-state assignment.
status: Molecular formal Pr(V) was isolated at low temperature in 2025. A 2026 ligand comparison found modest redox-potential changes but major stability differences, with some Pr(V) states observable only electrochemically.
why: Enables systematic high-valent lanthanide reactivity beyond specially protected examples.
key_works: A. C. Boggiano et al. (2025), “Praseodymium in the formal +5 oxidation state,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41557-025-01797-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-025-01797-w); T.-R. Nero et al. (2026), “Ligand Design Criteria for the Stability of High Oxidation State Praseodymium Complexes,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c05024](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c05024).

title: Electron source and structural trigger for Tb(IV) polyoxometalate auto-reduction
open: Identify the electron donor and structural changes causing Tb(IV)–W34 to reduce during desolvation. Distinguish this pathway from X-ray-induced reduction and use the mechanism to improve stability.
status: A 2026 Wells–Dawson complex retained its characteristic absorption for twelve days in capped water but lost its brown color on approximately ten-minute desolvation timescales. The aqueous complex is established; the desolvation-triggered reaction remains the mechanistic target.
why: Makes aqueous high-valent lanthanide compounds usable in isolated materials.
key_works: P. J. Subintoro et al. (2026), “Structural and spectroscopic characterization of a Tb(IV) polyoxometalate,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75657-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-75657-7).

title: Isolation of a molecular promethium(II) complex
open: Isolate a molecular Pm(II) complex and establish metal-centered reduction and coordination geometry independently of ligand-radical alternatives.
status: Anderson-Sanchez’s 2024 dissertation identifies Pm as the missing radioactive member of the molecular divalent-lanthanide series. The 2024 aqueous Pm–diglycolamide structure establishes Pm(III), leaving divalent isolation as a distinct target.
why: Supplies a missing test of how configuration and ligand symmetry control lanthanide reduction.
key_works: L. M. Anderson-Sanchez (2024), “Understanding the Role of Steric Factors in the Successful Isolation of Low Oxidation State Lanthanide and Actinide Complexes,” [doctoral dissertation](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/0nz1t51t); D. M. Driscoll et al. (2024), “Observation of a promethium complex in solution,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-07267-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07267-6).

title: Stepwise hydration energies and ligand-exchange kinetics of nobelium ions
open: Determine hydration binding energies and state-resolved ligand-exchange rates for mass-identified nobelium complexes. Separate intrinsic chemistry from formation and survival biases in the apparatus.
status: Pore and colleagues directly identified No-containing molecular species after exposure to water and nitrogen in 2025. Calibrated thermochemistry and exchange kinetics remain proposed extensions beyond molecular identification and relative production yields.
why: Provides quantitative late-actinide bonding tests using atom-at-a-time measurements.
key_works: J. L. Pore et al. (2025), “Direct identification of Ac and No molecules with an atom-at-a-time technique,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41586-025-09342-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09342-y).

title: Site-resolved explanation of flerovium’s two adsorption populations
open: Quantify contributions from weak terrace adsorption, surface diffusion, and trapping at rare active gold sites to flerovium deposition. Use characterized surfaces and independently testable kinetic predictions.
status: A 2022 study reconciled contrasting adsorption observations using inhomogeneous surfaces and a proposed two-stage mechanism. Experimental discrimination of the individual adsorption states remains the narrower unresolved target.
why: Separates intrinsic element reactivity from the microscopic structure of the detector.
key_works: A. Yakushev et al. (2022), “On the adsorption and reactivity of element 114, flerovium,” [DOI: 10.3389/fchem.2022.976635](https://doi.org/10.3389/fchem.2022.976635).

title: Direct chemical-form verification of chromatographed nihonium and moscovium
open: Determine directly whether transported and adsorbed Nh/Mc species are atoms, ions, or trace-impurity compounds. Link molecular identity to the measured chromatogram.
status: The 2024 experiment measured adsorption-enthalpy magnitudes near 58 and 54 kJ/mol and supported atomic assignments computationally. Direct mass-sensitive identification, developed for other heavy elements in 2025, remains a stronger proposed test.
why: Makes apparent relativistic reactivity trends independent of assumed chemical identity.
key_works: A. Yakushev et al. (2024), “Manifestation of relativistic effects in the chemical properties of nihonium and moscovium revealed by gas chromatography studies,” [DOI: 10.3389/fchem.2024.1474820](https://doi.org/10.3389/fchem.2024.1474820); F. H. Garcia et al. (2025), “Atom-at-a-Time Radioactive Molecule Identification: Looking toward Studies of Superheavy Elements,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpca.5c02098](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpca.5c02098).

title: Does oxygen-bound seaborgium hexaisocarbonyl exist as a metastable molecule?
open: Establish whether Sg(OC)₆ is a genuine metastable minimum after correlation, spin–orbit, and vibrational effects are included. Determine its isomerization lifetime and a distinguishing experimental signature if it is viable.
status: A 2023 Dirac–Fock/Breit–Gaunt study predicted the oxygen-bound isomer while finding Sg(CO)₆ more stable. An optimized octahedral structure and favorable atomization energy leave kinetic survival unresolved.
why: Tests unusual ligand connectivity at the relativistic edge of coordination chemistry.
key_works: G. L. Malli (2023), “Relativistic and magnetic Breit effects for the reaction Sg + 6CO → Sg(CO)6 and Sg(OC)6: Prediction of the existence and atomization energy of the isomer Sg(OC)6,” [DOI: 10.1063/5.0152081](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0152081).

title: Experimental test of uranium–chloride aggregation suppressing conductivity
open: Measure whether increasing AlCl₃ produces U–Cl–U and U–Cl–Al aggregates while increasing self-diffusion but decreasing conductivity. Resolve the ion-motion correlations responsible.
status: A 2026 ab initio study predicts chloride depletion, uranium polymerization, and eventual aluminium incorporation. Simultaneous structural and transport validation remains a proposed extension beyond the simulations.
why: Establishes when conductivity fails as a proxy for individual-ion mobility.
key_works: S. Wang et al. (2026), “AlCl3-induced aggregation of U-Cl complexes and its impact on the structure and thermodynamic properties of LiCl-KCl-AlCl3-UCl3 molten salts,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2026.156517](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnucmat.2026.156517).

title: Dose-dependent change of FLiBe fluoroacidity
open: Quantify how irradiation changes available fluoride and fluoroberyllate-network populations, including recovery kinetics. Determine whether those chemical changes explain altered metal corrosion.
status: Peterkin’s 2026 research abstract reports irradiation-emulating simulations showing structural changes, with quantification still forthcoming. The relationship among radiolysis, fluoroacidity, and corrosion remains explicitly incomplete.
why: Separates radiation-altered salt chemistry from thermal corrosion.
key_works: A. Peterkin (2026), “Modeling Radiolysis Effects in FLiBe Molten Fluoride Salt,” [DOE NNSA LRGF research abstract](https://www.krellinst.org/lrgf/conf/2026/abstracts/peterkin2024).

title: Experimental detection of hydride-like tritium in reducing FLiBe
open: Determine whether beryllium-associated hydride-like hydrogen isotopes form a measurable inventory alongside molecular hydrogen and hydrogen fluoride. Measure interconversion and release rates.
status: A 2026 molecular-dynamics study predicts negatively charged Be-associated hydrogen under reducing conditions. The chemical-state assignment still requires isotope-sensitive experimental validation.
why: Tests whether two-species transport models omit a retained tritium reservoir.
key_works: L. Jiang et al. (2026), “Atomic-scale insights into tritium speciation and interfacial behavior at molten salt/graphite and molten salt/alloy interfaces,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.ijhydene.2026.156188](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijhydene.2026.156188).

title: Neodymium(II) inventory during simultaneous irradiation and metal contact
open: Close the Nd(II)/Nd(III)/Nd-metal balance during simultaneous irradiation and metal contact. Distinguish radiolytic reduction from comproportionation and subsequent radical oxidation.
status: A 2026 study measured Nd(III) electron capture at 4.54 × 10¹⁰ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ at 673 K and raised concerns about the stability of Nd(II) produced through comproportionation. Simultaneous steady-state accounting remains a proposed test.
why: Makes fission-product valence a measured variable rather than an equilibrium assumption.
key_works: S. Castro Baldivieso et al. (2026), “Influence of Nd(II) and Nd(III) Ions on the Speciation and Kinetic Dynamics of Radiolytic Transients in Molten LiCl-KCl Eutectic Salt Mixtures,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c04788](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c04788).

title: Chlorine escape versus trichloride retention at molten-salt surfaces
open: Measure Cl₂/Cl₃⁻ interconversion and surface-escape yields following irradiation as melt Lewis acidity changes. Test whether bulk chlorobasicity predicts interfacial behavior.
status: The 2025 bulk/slab simulations identify salt-dependent chlorine chemistry and uncertainty about volatile products near interfaces. A 2026 study extends the Cl₂ probe to divalent-metal melts; calibrated interfacial branching remains open.
why: Predicts corrosive off-gas formation from measured melt chemistry.
key_works: H. H. Nguyen et al. (2025), “Chlorine gas and anion radical reactivity in molten salts and the link to chlorobasicity,” [DOI: 10.1039/D4CP03285C](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4CP03285C); Y. Chen et al. (2026), “Chlorine Gas as a Lewis Acid–Base Probe for Molten Salts of Divalent Metal Ions,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcb.6c01313](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcb.6c01313).

title: Ordering the americium and curium deposition potentials in LiCl–KCl
open: Resolve which of the Am(II)/Am and Cm(III)/Cm equilibrium potentials is more positive in a common calibrated LiCl–KCl melt. Reduce uncertainty below their separation.
status: Potapov’s 2026 IAEA contribution reports literature values spanning −2.83 to −2.89 V versus Cl₂/Cl⁻ at 500 °C and explicitly states that even their ordering is unclear.
why: Establishes whether assumed electrochemical selectivity has a thermodynamic basis.
key_works: A. Potapov (2026), “Chemical Separation of Americium and Curium in Molten Salts: Thermodynamic Modeling,” [IAEA FR26 contribution](https://conferences.iaea.org/event/436/contributions/39492/).

title: From telluride formation thresholds to grain-boundary tellurium flux
open: Predict tellurium entry into alloy grain boundaries from salt redox, dissolved tellurium species, and surface-telluride chemistry. Separate surface-scale growth from embrittling inward transport.
status: A 2026 study established potential-dependent nickel tellurization and acceleration by CrF₃-containing fluoride melt. The quantitative connection to grain-boundary transport remains a proposed extension.
why: Connects melt chemistry to a specific loss-of-ductility mechanism.
key_works: R. Wu et al. (2026), “How the presence of molten fluoride salt influences the tellurization of UNS N10003 alloy?” [DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2026.156438](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnucmat.2026.156438).

title: Redox-resolved iodine volatility above multicomponent fluoride melts
open: Measure partitioning among dissolved iodide complexes, molecular iodine, and iodine-bearing vapor during oxidizing transients. Determine release kinetics in addition to equilibrium phase behavior.
status: A 2025 assessment models the Li/Na/K/Cs–F/I reciprocal system. Argonne’s source-term work identifies higher-temperature and more-oxidizing iodine release as a prediction need; coupled redox–volatility validation remains a proposed target.
why: Makes iodine-release estimates depend on measured chemical processes.
key_works: C. M. Dixon et al. (2025), “Thermodynamic assessment of the Li, Na, K, Cs | F, I reciprocal salt for MSR applications,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.jct.2025.107548](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jct.2025.107548); S. Shahbazi et al. (2023), “Progress on Long-Term Objectives for the Development of Advanced Reactor Mechanistic Source Term Modeling and Simulation Tools,” [ANL/NSE-23/79](https://publications.anl.gov/anlpubs/2024/12/185813.pdf).

title: Chemical pathway from the acetate-stabilized Pu₆ cluster to primary PuO₂ particles
open: Identify ligand-loss and condensation intermediates converting [Pu₆O₄(OH)₄]¹²⁺ into primary PuO₂ colloids. Distinguish that conversion from subsequent aggregation.
status: A 2026 year-scale study found local Pu–Pu coordination consistent with small primary particles but SAXS diameters reaching 10–15 nm. It supports primary-particle formation followed by aggregation; direct intermediate and rate assignment remains open.
why: Predicts when molecular precursors become transportable colloidal material.
key_works: M. Munoz et al. (2026), “Unveiling the Stability and Kinetic Pathway from Plutonium Clusters to Colloidal PuO2 Nanoparticles,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c05921](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c05921).

title: Complete ligand identities of native nonpertechnetate tank-waste species
open: Assign coordination ligands and molecular structures to low-valent technetium fractions in untreated alkaline tank waste. Quantify transformations introduced by sample processing.
status: AN-102 measurements identified Tc(I) carbonyl and Tc(IV) species in 2020; a 2024 AP-105/AP-107 study added Tc(VI). Positive identification of resin-interacting and unretained species remains incomplete beyond those oxidation-state assignments.
why: Enables treatment of the species escaping pertechnetate-specific capture.
key_works: S. Chatterjee et al. (2020), “Identification and Quantification of Technetium Species in Hanford Waste Tank AN-102,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c02864](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.analchem.0c02864); R. M. Asmussen et al. (2024), “The simultaneous removal of technetium and iodine from Hanford tank waste,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.cej.2024.151449](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cej.2024.151449).

title: Nonpertechnetate oxidation fronts after grout reducing capacity is consumed
open: Predict coupled oxidation and release of initially reduced technetium as oxygen ingress exhausts slag-derived reducing capacity. Retain dependence on the starting Tc species.
status: A 2026 real-waste study found over 80% conversion of released nonpertechnetate to pertechnetate and slower oxidation/release with blast-furnace slag. Lifetime prediction across an advancing redox front remains an extrapolative target.
why: Tests whether favorable initial retention persists after binder redox conditions change.
key_works: A. R. Lawter et al. (2026), “The Leaching Behavior of Non-Pertechnetate Species in Cementitious Waste Forms,” [DOI: 10.1021/acsearthspacechem.5c00222](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsearthspacechem.5c00222).

title: Atomic branching between peroxide-driven UO₂ dissolution and decomposition
open: Measure surface intermediates and branching probabilities determining whether radiolytic H₂O₂ oxidatively dissolves UO₂ or decomposes catalytically. Resolve defect and carbonate dependence.
status: A 2026 DFT+U study proposes competing pathways and a 0.69 eV initial O–O-cleavage barrier on UO₂(111). Intermediate-resolved kinetic validation under aqueous conditions remains a proposed extension.
why: Connects oxidant production to actual fuel-matrix release.
key_works: Y. Yu et al. (2026), “Mechanisms of initial oxidation and catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide on the uranium dioxide (111) surface: A DFT+U study,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2026.156658](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnucmat.2026.156658).

title: AmSel selectivity through repeated accumulation of TODGA degradation products
open: Predict and maintain Am/Cm separation through repeated solvent reuse with a changing mixture of TODGA fragments. Measure fragment accumulation and each fragment’s metal-binding contribution.
status: A 2025 study examined individual and combined degradation products and adjustments to stripping conditions. Long-run closure of degradation, regeneration, and selectivity remains a proposed systems extension.
why: Makes extractant radiation resistance meaningful over a process lifetime.
key_works: P. Vacas-Arquero, I. Sánchez-García, and H. Galán (2025), “Influence of the accumulation of TODGA degradation compounds in the separation of Americium from Curium by the AmSel process,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.pnucene.2025.105677](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pnucene.2025.105677).

title: Predicting methyl-iodide capture by chemically aged silver mordenite
open: Predict breakthrough from measured populations of metallic silver, exchanged Ag(I), and nitrate species after variable NOₓ/moisture histories. Account for iodine capture by each population.
status: A 2020 study identified oxidation and inward silver migration, with nitrates carrying up to 95% of capacity in well-aged samples. A 2024 study adds moisture and storage effects; prospective state-to-breakthrough prediction remains open.
why: Replaces fresh-sorbent capacity assumptions with chemically informed lifetime prediction.
key_works: H. Goettsche et al. (2024), “Effects of moisture and aging upon decomposition of methyl iodide by reduced silver mordenite,” [DOI: 10.1007/s10450-024-00473-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10450-024-00473-8); A. I. Wiechert et al. (2020), “Capture of Iodine from Nuclear-Fuel-Reprocessing Off-Gas: Influence of Aging on a Reduced Silver Mordenite Adsorbent after Exposure to NO/NO2,” [DOI: 10.1021/acsami.0c15456](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.0c15456).

title: Origin of humidity inhibition in methyl-iodide decomposition on silver mordenite
open: Distinguish water blocking reactant adsorption from product-desorption limitation as the cause of humidity inhibition. If retained products control the rate, identify them and measure their desorption kinetics.
status: The 2024 experiments found approximately 30% slower apparent decomposition under humid conditions. Goettsche’s 2025 dissertation also leaves the rate-limiting step and practical working capacity unresolved because catalytic conversion can obscure iodine retention.
why: Makes disappearance of CH₃I an interpretable measurement of conversion and capture.
key_works: H. Goettsche et al. (2024), “Effects of moisture and aging upon decomposition of methyl iodide by reduced silver mordenite,” [DOI: 10.1007/s10450-024-00473-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10450-024-00473-8); H. Goettsche (2025), “Investigations into methyl iodide adsorption and decomposition on reduced silver mordenite,” [doctoral dissertation](https://verso.uidaho.edu/esploro/outputs/doctoral/Investigations-into-methyl-iodide-adsorption-and/996825066201851).

title: The missing aluminacyclopropene in aluminium-catalysed alkyne trimerization
open: Observe the proposed initial Al–C–C three-membered intermediate, or experimentally exclude it in favor of an alternative pathway. Establish its lifetime and productive catalytic flux.
status: Zhang and Liu’s 2026 catalyst reaches 2,290 turnovers. Their primary account reports downstream aluminacycles without detectable intermediate X even at 1:1 Al:alkyne stoichiometry; calculated onward barriers are below 8 kcal/mol.
why: Identifies the first bond-forming event and opportunities to control ring formation.
key_works: X. Zhang and L. L. Liu (2026), “Aluminium redox catalysis enables cyclotrimerization of alkynes,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41586-025-09941-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09941-9); their 2025 primary preprint, “Aluminum Redox Catalysis: Reppe Cyclotrimerization of Alkynes,” [DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-5825959/v2](https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-5825959/v2).

title: Direct accounting of the Ge(III) radical partner during azoarene hydrogenation
open: Measure the Ge-centered radical cation and azoarene radical anion simultaneously during hydrogenation, with calibrated concentrations and lifetimes. Determine branching into hydrogen transfer, recombination, and escape.
status: The 2025 work detected azoarene radical anions by EPR and characterized a TEMPO-derived product supporting Ge(III). Quantitative observation of both radical partners during turnover remains missing.
why: Distinguishes productive single-electron chemistry from radical leakage.
key_works: Y. Zhou et al. (2025), “Germanium-Mediated Catalysis via Ge(II)/Ge(III)/Ge(IV) or Ge(II)/Ge(IV) Redox Cycling,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.5c12407](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c12407).

title: High-turnover elemental-germanium bromoalkylation with a closed inventory
open: Develop mechanically activated elemental Ge for alkene bromoalkylation with measured recovery and losses. A proposed engineering milestone is at least 100 cumulative turnovers without continuous net consumption of the Ge inventory.
status: Guo and colleagues demonstrated activation and catalytic bromoalkylation in 2025, alongside separate Ge recycling experiments. The 100-turnover criterion with a complete inventory is a proposed assessment, not a reported record.
why: Establishes whether elemental Ge can function as a reusable process material.
key_works: G. Guo et al. (2025), “Elemental Germanium Activation and Catalysis Enabled by Mechanical Force,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.202421446](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202421446).

title: Cyclodigermoxane resting state versus irreversible oxygen trap
open: Measure monomer–dimer equilibria and oxygen-transfer rates of Ge(IV) oxo species during catalysis. Determine when cyclodigermoxane is regenerable and when it becomes a catalyst sink.
status: Liu and colleagues isolated Ge and Sn oxo products and demonstrated nitrous-oxide activation in 2025. Their differing subsequent reduction chemistry motivates this proposed kinetic test.
why: Locates the regeneration barrier limiting germanium’s accessible chemistry.
key_works: Z. Liu et al. (2025), “EII/EIVO (E = Ge, Sn) Catalyzed Nitrous Oxide Activation and Chemodivergent Reduction of Nitroarenes,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.202515638](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202515638).

title: A measured four-product branching network for stannylene nitroarene reduction
open: Determine elementary rates and catalyst populations that predict amine, hydroxylamine, azoxy, and hydrazine selectivity in the Sn(II)/Sn(IV) system. Validate predictions on conditions excluded from fitting.
status: The 2025 report demonstrates all four product classes and proposes mechanisms. A measured, prospectively tested branching model remains the proposed target.
why: Enables predictive control of nitrogen oxidation state and N–N coupling.
key_works: Z. Liu et al. (2025), “EII/EIVO (E = Ge, Sn) Catalyzed Nitrous Oxide Activation and Chemodivergent Reduction of Nitroarenes,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.202515638](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202515638).

title: Observable tests of electron redistribution during silicon insertion into Zn–Zn
open: Determine which spectroscopic and electron-density changes distinguish competing descriptions of silylene insertion into Zn–Zn. Test those predictions across substituted complexes using observable electron redistribution.
