status: The 2025 report described reductive addition; a 2026 wavefunction analysis supports redox-neutral insertion. An observable-calibrated comparison remains a proposed experimental target; formal oxidation state itself is a model assignment.
why: Tests when redox terminology predicts main-group reactivity.
key_works: W. Yang et al. (2025), “Reactions of a Zn–Zn bond with main group carbene analogues as a prototypical case of reductive addition,” [DOI: 10.1038/s44160-025-00790-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44160-025-00790-y); P. Belanzoni, G. Comas-Vilà, and D. Sorbelli (2026), “Diagnosing the Redox Character of Bond Activation by Main Group Centers: Reductive Addition vs Redox-Neutral Insertion as a Case Study,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.6c01103](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.6c01103).

title: The nickel hydride behind additive-switched silylene–Ni hydrosilylation
open: Identify the active Ni species generated by nBuLi from the bis(silylene)-pincer Ni(II) chloride precursor. Determine whether intact pincer-bound Ni–H accounts for Markovnikov selectivity.
status: A 2026 paper reports opposite regioselectivity with nBuLi and KOtBu. It suggests a nickel hydride as the active catalyst under the former conditions without establishing its structure and abundance.
why: Distinguishes ligand-controlled selectivity from additive-induced catalyst reconstruction.
key_works: Z. Yang et al. (2026), “Additive-controlled selective hydrosilylation of aryl alkenes catalyzed by bis(silylene) pincer nickel(II) chloride,” [DOI: 10.1039/D5NJ03998C](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5NJ03998C).

title: Recovering the borylene framework after dinitrogen-derived ammonium release
open: Identify boron-containing products from acid release of ammonium in the CAAC-supported diborylene system. Regenerate the original nitrogen-binding framework with closed boron and ligand balances.
status: Stoichiometric room-temperature N₂-to-NH₄Cl conversion was achieved in 2020. The 2026 mechanistic study still describes an incompletely characterized boron mixture after HCl workup; recovery from that workup remains a proposed engineering target.
why: Exposes the regeneration cost independently of the already demonstrated nitrogen reduction.
key_works: M.-A. Légaré et al. (2020), “One-pot, room-temperature conversion of dinitrogen to ammonium chloride at a main-group element,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41557-020-0520-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-020-0520-6); S. Yu and M. B. Hall (2026), “Mechanism of Dinitrogen Reduction in a Borylene Complex by Density Functional Theory,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c04644](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c04644).

title: Experimental tests of boron-protonated dead ends in diborylene N₂ reduction
open: Test whether stronger acids and weaker reductants populate B-protonated alternatives to productive N-protonated species. Measure whether proton migration or further reduction returns them to the productive sequence.
status: Yu and Hall’s 2026 calculations predict favorable B-protonated isomers with substantial proton-migration barriers. Their structures and kinetic importance remain experimentally unresolved.
why: Explains reagent-dependent failure and trapping of reducing equivalents.
key_works: S. Yu and M. B. Hall (2026), “Mechanism of Dinitrogen Reduction in a Borylene Complex by Density Functional Theory,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c04644](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c04644).

title: Solution-phase N₂ capture by a designed silylene–borole frustrated Lewis pair
open: Synthesize a predicted silylene–borole pair and demonstrate solution-phase N₂ binding and activation. Establish structural identity, reaction rate, and equilibrium constant.
status: The 2025 designs predict barriers of 16.9–22.5 kcal/mol and reaction free energies of −32.3 to −36.7 kcal/mol. N₂ cleavage by SiH₂ in a cryogenic matrix was demonstrated in 2024; the designed solution chemistry remains untested.
why: Tests whether aromaticity-driven cooperativity survives synthesis and solvent effects.
key_works: S. Dong, W. Wang, and J. Zhu (2025), “Design of Borole- and Silylene-Based Frustrated Lewis Pairs for Dinitrogen Activation Promoted by Aromaticity: A Combined DFT and Machine Learning Study,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c02343](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c02343); L. Cai et al. (2024), “N2 cleavage by silylene and formation of H2Si(μ-N)2SiH2,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-48064-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-48064-z).

title: Diazo-cleavage product release that preserves the carborane bis(silylene)
open: Release nitrogen-derived products from the Si═N–Si–N═CAr₂ adduct while retaining and regenerating its carborane-supported bis(silylene) framework. Account for both nitrogen atoms and silicon-containing products.
status: The 2026 work demonstrates diazo N═N scission. Hydrolysis releases imine and ammonia but also silica, carborane, and ligand-derived material; framework-preserving release remains a proposed extension.
why: Determines whether cooperative silicon cleavage can become a repeated transformation.
key_works: Y. Xiong, S. Yao, and M. Driess (2026), “Bis(silylene)-Mediated N═N Bond Scission of Diazo Compounds,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.3873649](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.3873649).

title: Productive turnover beyond imidosilane ligand-migration redox shuttling
open: Couple borylsilylene/imidosilane interconversion to release of a nitrogen-transfer product while restoring the initial silicon coordination and ligand inventory. Demonstrate repeated net substrate conversion.
status: Tang and colleagues established reversible Si(IV)/Si(II) shuttling and isolable, nearly thermoneutral isomers in 2025. A product-releasing nitrogen-transfer cycle remains a proposed target.
why: Tests whether internal ligand migration can support catalysis without consuming the framework.
key_works: J. Tang, Y. Wang, A. E. Crumpton, C. McManus, and S. Aldridge (2025), “Isomerisation and Insertion Chemistry of Imidosilanes Enabled by Reversible Si(IV)/Si(II) Redox Shuttling,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.202505872](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202505872).

title: Regenerating the CAAC–boron site after ammonia N–H addition
open: Reverse or productively exploit ammonia addition across the CAAC-carbon–boron unit, restoring the reactive framework after nitrogen transfer. Determine whether the carbon-bound proton can be removed without framework destruction.
status: The 2026 transient-borylene chemistry produces a CAAC-carbon-protonated aminoborane from ammonia. Regeneration and repeated use of this particular ligand-assisted activation mode remain proposed follow-on targets.
why: Establishes whether CAAC participation is reversible cooperation or a stoichiometric ligand sink.
key_works: M. Weber, S. Kar, P. Joos, R. D. Dewhurst, and H. Braunschweig (2026), “N–H/P–H bond activation of ammonia, amines and phosphines at a transient borylene,” [DOI: 10.1039/D6SC00526H](https://doi.org/10.1039/D6SC00526H).

title: A bottleable triplet phosphinidene that avoids intramolecular arene addition
open: Isolate a free, monocoordinate triplet phosphinidene in a hydrindacene-type environment while suppressing reaction with its own aryl framework. Establish its spin state, identity, and solution persistence.
status: The 2024 attempt instead produced singlet phosphanorcaradiene through intramolecular dearomatization. This failed triplet isolation is still discussed in 2026 primary literature; isolated singlet phosphinidenes and precursor equivalents do not fulfill this specific target.
why: Exposes phosphorus-centered triplet chemistry without precursor-release equilibria.
key_works: Y. Chen, P. Su, D. Wang, Z. Ke, and G. Tan (2024), “Molecular-strain induced phosphinidene reactivity of a phosphanorcaradiene,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-49042-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-49042-1).

title: Does diarylbismuth azide photolysis produce a discrete bismuth nitrene?
open: Establish whether photolysis generates a separately populated bismuth–nitrene species. Determine its electronic state and lifetime, distinguishing it from pathways giving the same trapping products.
status: Pugliese and colleagues’ 2026 ultrafast and trapping experiments support nitrene-equivalent reactivity but explicitly do not establish a discrete bismuth nitrene unambiguously.
why: Identifies the electronic structure responsible for heavy-pnictogen nitrogen transfer.
key_works: G. Pugliese, O. Pichl, G. Schnakenburg, P. Vöhringer, L. I. Domenianni, and A. Bismuto (2026), “Photochemical and Thermal Activation of a Diarylbismuth Azide,” [DOI: 10.1002/chem.71556](https://doi.org/10.1002/chem.71556).

title: Direct detection of the open-shell iminobismuthane amination sequence
open: Detect the proposed nitrogen-centered radical and carbon-radical partner during photoactive iminobismuthane C–H amination. Test whether in-cage electron transfer precedes C–N bond formation.
status: Catalytic amination was demonstrated in 2026 with a proposed sequence involving ligand-to-ligand charge transfer, hydrogen abstraction, and in-cage electron transfer. Detection of the putative open-shell intermediates remained ongoing.
why: Distinguishes radical recombination from radical-to-polar crossover.
key_works: T. Tsuruta et al. (2026), “Photoactive Iminobismuthanes for Catalytic C–H Amination,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.6c04805](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.6c04805).

title: The fleeting Sb(III) hydride in disulfide hydroboration
open: Measure the population and lifetime of the proposed hydridostibine between borane metathesis and Sb(I) regeneration. Obtain kinetic evidence discriminating a separately populated hydride from a concerted alternative.
status: The 2024 paper establishes Sb(I)/Sb(III) disulfide-hydroboration turnover and proposes the reaction sequence. Direct hydride-population measurements are a proposed mechanistic test of that account.
why: Tests the elementary event assigned to Sb–H formation and subsequent elimination.
key_works: M. Huang, K. Li, Z. Zhang, and J. Zhou (2024), “Antimony Redox Catalysis: Hydroboration of Disulfides through Unique Sb(I)/Sb(III) Redox Cycling,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.4c05905](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.4c05905).

title: One-electron versus two-electron flux in antimonate–NHPI aerobic coupling
open: Quantify contributions from Sb-centered single-electron oxidation, PINO-mediated hydrogen abstraction, and the proposed two-electron antimonate pathway. Identify antimony states populated during turnover.
status: The 2013 report explicitly left the roles of antimonate and NHPI unclear. Coupling persisted at 21% yield with a radical inhibitor, motivating an alternative pathway without establishing its structure or flux.
why: Determines whether a catalytic counteranion operates through one mechanism or several.
key_works: A. Tanoue, W.-J. Yoo, and S. Kobayashi (2013), “Antimony/N-Hydroxyphthalimide as a Catalyst System for Cross-Dehydrogenative Coupling Reactions under Aerobic Conditions,” [DOI: 10.1002/adsc.201200999](https://doi.org/10.1002/adsc.201200999).

title: The transient silane–silylium ion in stibenium-catalysed Si–C redistribution
open: Detect or kinetically discriminate the proposed [Et₂HSi···H–SiEt₃]⁺ intermediate during constrained-stibenium silane redistribution. Establish whether it carries exchange between Et₃SiH and Et₂SiH₂/Et₄Si.
status: The 2026 work demonstrates Si–C activation and identifies Sb(V) species supporting the cycle. The short-lived silane–silylium carrier remains proposed.
why: Distinguishes antimony-centered exchange from cationic silicon propagation.
key_works: D. Toami and R. Dobrovetsky (2026), “Structurally Constrained Stibenium: Metallomimetic C−Si Bond Activation,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.3059944](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.3059944).

title: The unactivated-alkene polarity boundary in bismuth alkyl-Heck photocatalysis
open: Determine competing rates responsible for failure of unactivated alkenes in the demonstrated bismuth alkyl-Heck system. Establish productive coupling while controlling radical oligomerization.
status: The 2025 primary report identifies unactivated alkenes as outside the protocol and attributes the boundary to polarity mismatch. Ordinary styrenes already work in its alkyl-coupling branch.
why: Tests the practical substrate boundary imposed by radical polarity.
key_works: S. Ni, A. Stamoulis, V. A. Béland, and J. Cornella (2025), “Bismuth-photocatalysed Heck-type coupling with alkyl and aryl electrophiles,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41929-025-01438-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-025-01438-y).

title: Solution persistence of the o-benzoquinone–AsN complex
open: Generate the weak o-benzoquinone–AsN complex in solution. Measure its lifetime and intermolecular trapping before recombination to arsinonitrene.
status: This specific complex was characterized in a 10 K argon matrix in 2026. A different NHC-stabilized AsN adduct was already isolated in 2020; the open target concerns the weak quinone complex.
why: Exposes reactive AsN chemistry without a confining matrix.
key_works: W. Qian, M. E. Sandoval-Salinas, R. Crespo-Otero, P. R. Schreiner, and A. Mardyukov (2026), “Synthesis of an o-Benzoquinone Arsenic Mononitride (As≡N) Complex and Its Reaction to Singlet Arsinonitrene,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.5c20377](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c20377); D. Bockfeld and M. Tamm (2020), “Isolation of N-Heterocyclic Carbene-Stabilized Phosphorus and Arsenic Mononitride,” [DOI: 10.1002/zaac.202000094](https://doi.org/10.1002/zaac.202000094).

title: An isolable molecular antimony-mononitride adduct
open: Stabilize an intact SbN unit in an isolable molecular adduct. Establish its bonding and isotope-sensitive vibrational signature.
status: Gas-phase SbN spectroscopy dates to Coy and Sponer’s 1940 experiments. Qian and colleagues’ 2026 primary comparison lists SbN as detected but not isolated.
why: Isolable samples would test how coordination stabilizes a heavy-element nitride.
key_works: N. H. Coy and H. Sponer (1940), “Emission Spectrum of Antimony Nitride,” [DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.58.709](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.58.709); W. Qian et al. (2026), “Synthesis of an o-Benzoquinone Arsenic Mononitride (As≡N) Complex and Its Reaction to Singlet Arsinonitrene,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.5c20377](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c20377).

title: An isolable molecular bismuth-mononitride adduct
open: Prepare a molecular BiN adduct stable outside a molecular beam or cryogenic matrix. Measure its multiple-bond character.
status: Gas-phase BiN rotational and hyperfine structure were measured in 2004. Qian and colleagues’ 2026 primary comparison lists BiN as detected but not isolated.
why: Provides material for testing relativistic bonding and exploring molecular nitride precursors.
key_works: S. A. Cooke, J. M. Michaud, and M. C. L. Gerry (2004), “Microwave spectra, nuclear field shift effects, geometries and hyperfine constants of bismuth mononitride, BiN, and bismuth monophosphide, BiP,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.molstruc.2003.10.049](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molstruc.2003.10.049); W. Qian et al. (2026), [AsN study and comparative Table 1](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c20377).

title: A free phosphatetrazolate [PN₄]⁻ ring
open: Release and isolate aromatic [PN₄]⁻ from its metal coordination environment without nitrogen loss or P–N fragmentation. Determine its counterion dependence and decomposition kinetics.
status: An osmium-bound PN₄ ring was formed in 2025 through phosphorus-mononitride chemistry. Metal-free isolation remains a proposed next target; HCPN₃⁻ and P₂N₃⁻ are different compositions.
why: Tests whether aromatic stabilization sustains this nitrogen-rich phosphorus heterocycle independently.
key_works: S. Edin et al. (2025), “Unleashing phosphorus mononitride,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-60669-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-60669-6).

title: Germylene regeneration after photoinduced benzene scission
open: Release carbon fragments produced by the long-lived triplet germylene’s benzene cleavage and restore the germylene for another cycle. Close germanium, ligand, and reducing-equivalent inventories.
status: The 2026 germylene has a room-temperature triplet half-life of about 14 hours and performs stoichiometric doubly reductive benzene scission. Product release and repeated cleavage remain proposed engineering targets.
why: Determines whether a persistent excited main-group center can support repeated arene deconstruction.
key_works: E. Soto et al. (2026), “A photoexcited triplet state germylene with a half-life of hours at room temperature,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41557-026-02153-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-026-02153-2).

title: Monomeric solution photophysics of Sn(tBu-pdp-tBu)
open: Measure the excited-state spectrum, lifetime, and radiative/nonradiative rates of monomeric Sn(tBu-pdp-tBu) in solution. Distinguish the monomer from bridged dimers and determine whether its solid-state emissive state survives.
status: The 2026 study establishes red triplet ligand-to-metal charge-transfer emission in the solid. Bridged-dimer formation prevented the corresponding solution investigation.
why: Separates intrinsic molecular behavior from aggregation and crystal packing.
key_works: P. Sikora, R. Naumann, K. Heinze, and C. Förster (2026), “Ligand Topology Tunes Energy and Character of Emissive Triplet States in Stannylenes,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.6c01229](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.6c01229).

title: The hydridophosphorane in trialkylphosphine-catalysed C–F cleavage
open: Observe hydride transfer to phosphorus and the ensuing hydridophosphorane during pentafluoropyridine hydrodefluorination. Test whether its decay supplies C–H product at the catalytic rate.
status: The 2024 work observes phosphonium intermediates and computationally supports fluorosilicate-mediated hydride delivery followed by reductive elimination. The proposed phosphorus hydride still lacks a direct kinetic assignment during turnover.
why: Tests the central bond-making step of the simple-phosphine redox cycle.
key_works: S. Bonfante, C. Lorber, J. M. Lynam, A. Simonneau, and J. M. Slattery (2024), “Metallomimetic C–F Activation Catalysis by Simple Phosphines,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.3c10614](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.3c10614).

title: The initiating reductant and oxygen inhibition in SF₆ photolysis with tBuOK/DMF
open: Identify the species transferring the first electron to SF₆ under visible irradiation of tBuOK/DMF. Measure how oxygen suppresses its formation or quenches it, discriminating an excited DMF-derived anion from alternative reductants.
status: Complete SF₆ defluorination under ambient conditions was demonstrated in 2026. Air inhibits conversion while nitrogen does not; the initiating reductant remains incompletely assigned.
why: Identifies the solvent chemistry controlling efficiency and oxygen sensitivity.
key_works: H. Zhang, Y.-M. Chen, S.-Y. Zhang, and Y.-B. Kang (2026), “Visible-light-driven photoreductive complete degradation of sulfur hexafluoride under ambient conditions,” [DOI: 10.1039/D6CC00483K](https://doi.org/10.1039/D6CC00483K).

title: Chloride-versus-sulfate pathway flux in cinnabar blackening
open: Measure contributions of chloride-assisted and sulfate-mediated pathways to HgS conversion into metallic mercury under museum illumination. Close the mercury balance across pigment, binder, secondary salts, and vapor.
status: Metallic mercury was directly demonstrated in photoaged cinnabar tempera in 2021, including a chloride-free pathway. Relative pathway fluxes under ordinary display conditions remain a proposed narrower target.
why: Identifies which environmental intervention slows a particular cinnabar paint.
key_works: K. Elert, M. Pérez Mendoza, and C. Cardell (2021), “Direct evidence for metallic mercury causing photo-induced darkening of red cinnabar tempera paints,” [DOI: 10.1038/s42004-021-00610-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-021-00610-2).

title: Molecular identity of emerald-green photo-oxidation products
open: Determine stoichiometry, coordination, hydration, and connectivity of the amorphous As(V)-rich products formed during illumination. Distinguish copper arsenates, mixed-cation products, and organically associated arsenate.
status: A 2025 study separated light-driven surface oxidation from humidity-driven arsenolite formation. It explicitly left the structure and stoichiometry of the predominantly amorphous As(V) products unresolved.
why: Product identity determines whether arsenic remains immobilized or migrates.
key_works: S. Carboni Marri et al. (2025), “Discovering the dual degradation pathway of emerald green in oil paints: The effects of light and humidity,” [DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.ady1807](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ady1807).

title: Electron acceptor in emerald-green photo-oxidation
open: Identify what accepts the electrons when pigment As(III) becomes As(V). Quantify reduced products and resolve possible roles of transient Cu(I), oxygen, acetate, and other organic components.
status: The 2025 experiments found Cu(II) at the endpoint and arsenic oxidation without an oil binder. Acetate modification suggested a possible partner, but neither that pathway nor transient Cu(I) was demonstrated.
why: A balanced mechanism identifies inhibitors and oxygen-dependent pathways.
key_works: S. Carboni Marri et al. (2025), “Discovering the dual degradation pathway of emerald green in oil paints: The effects of light and humidity,” [DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.ady1807](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ady1807).

title: Sulfur mass balance during orpiment deterioration
open: Quantify sulfur released from deteriorating As₂S₃ as H₂S, dissolved reduced sulfur, oxidized sulfur, and binder-retained species. Link each sulfur pathway to the corresponding arsenic transformation.
status: Broers and colleagues established two arsenic-degradation pathways in 2023 but explicitly excluded sulfur fate from their study. Earlier H₂S suggestions do not establish its yield or competing sinks.
why: Mobile sulfur products can alter neighboring pigments.
key_works: F. T. H. Broers et al. (2023), “Two Pathways for the Degradation of Orpiment Pigment (As2S3) Found in Paintings,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.2c12271](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.2c12271).

title: Ambient reactive-oxygen dose controlling orpiment loss
open: Measure oxidant formation rates and reaction yields inside illuminated orpiment paint. Predict pigment loss from radical and peroxide fluxes under realistic binder, oxygen, and humidity conditions.
status: A 2025 model study compared four reactive oxygen species and found particularly strong deterioration with hydroxyl radicals. Their actual production and relative contributions inside artworks remain a proposed measurement target.
why: Connects reactive-species chemistry to practical illumination and atmosphere controls.
key_works: J. Sun et al. (2025), “Mechanistic Study on Orpiment Pigment Discoloration Induced by Reactive Oxygen Species,” [DOI: 10.3390/molecules30163318](https://doi.org/10.3390/molecules30163318).

title: Cadmium-sulfide defect signatures that predict future fading
open: Establish which CdS trap-state signatures predict subsequent oxidation rather than merely correlate with existing damage. Prospectively predict fading rates across independently prepared pigment formulations.
status: A 2019 Picasso-paint study connected preservation differences with photoluminescence and suggested a role for low crystallinity. A causal defect assignment and calibrated future-damage predictor remain proposed targets.
why: Identifies vulnerable cadmium paint before visible bleaching.
key_works: D. Comelli et al. (2019), “Degradation of Cadmium Yellow Paint: New Evidence from Photoluminescence Studies of Trap States in Picasso’s Femme (Époque des ‘Demoiselles d’Avignon’),” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.analchem.8b04914](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.analchem.8b04914).

title: Ultramarine sites initiating binder photoradicals
open: Identify the sulfur center, framework defect, or surface state initiating radical damage in ultramarine-containing binders. Connect site assignment to an action spectrum and selective suppression.
status: The 2017 work demonstrated light-induced binder deterioration while pigment remained intact. It established a route to ultramarine disease without assigning the initiating active site.
why: Targeted passivation could preserve both color and binder integrity.
key_works: E. R. de la Rie et al. (2017), “Photo-catalytic degradation of binding media of ultramarine blue containing paint layers: A new perspective on the phenomenon of ‘ultramarine disease’ in paintings,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.polymdegradstab.2017.08.002](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.polymdegradstab.2017.08.002).

title: Structural reversibility of Prussian-blue fading cycles
open: Determine whether recovered blue color also means restored Fe coordination, vacancy distribution, and cyanide framework. Follow repeated fading–reoxidation cycles to detect accumulated structural damage.
status: The 2014 textile study observed color recovery after three years in dark air but explicitly left post-recovery structural reversibility unresolved.
why: Establishes whether visually reversible fading conceals irreversible damage.
key_works: C. Gervais et al. (2014), “Light and anoxia fading of Prussian blue dyed textiles,” [publisher article](https://www.nature.com/articles/BMCs40494-014-0026-x).

title: Potassium sinks controlling smalt dealkalinization
open: Quantify potassium partitioning among mobile ions, carboxylates, alum-like phases, and other binder-associated reservoirs as smalt loses alkali. Predict how those sinks affect further leaching and cobalt coordination.
status: Combined K- and Co-edge XANES in 2024 showed formulation-dependent alteration and suggested potassium alum in historical material. Quantitative sink-controlled kinetics remain a proposed extension.
why: Explains why similar smalt formulations can age differently.
key_works: C. de Mecquenem et al. (2024), “Influence of the painting medium on the alteration process of smalt in oil paintings studied using combined K and Co K-edge XANES,” [DOI: 10.1007/s00339-024-07943-4](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00339-024-07943-4).

title: Peroxo versus oxide contributions to copper-resinate browning
open: Determine the abundance and optical contribution of peroxide-containing copper complexes and CuO in naturally browned copper-resinate paints. Reproduce native spectra from independently measured species concentrations.
status: A 2019 study supported a photochemical peroxo-complex explanation; a 2020 study proposed CuO formation under basic conditions. Their relative contributions in historical glazes remain a proposed discriminating target.
why: The competing products imply different preventative strategies.
key_works: M. Alter et al. (2019), “Photochemical Origin of the Darkening of Copper Acetate and Resinate Pigments in Historical Paintings,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.9b02007](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.9b02007); S. W. C. Horn et al. (2020), “Examination of the composition and mechanism of discoloration of the fugitive pigment copper resinate,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.ica.2019.119407](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ica.2019.119407).

title: Water’s catalytic step in zinc-soap crystallization
open: Identify the coordination-changing step through which trace water accelerates zinc-carboxylate crystallization in cured oil. Measure the relevant intermediate, water dependence, and possible catalytic turnover.
status: In 2023, swelling alone did not cause the acceleration, while water-containing solvent induced crystallization. Stabilization of transient charged states was proposed without direct observation of the intermediate.
why: Explains why small water impurities in treatment solvents reorganize metal soaps.
key_works: J. Hermans, K. Helwig, S. Woutersen, and K. Keune (2023), “Traces of water catalyze zinc soap crystallization in solvent-exposed oil paints,” [DOI: 10.1039/D2CP04861B](https://doi.org/10.1039/D2CP04861B).

title: Zinc-soap polymorph selection inside heterogeneous oil networks
open: Predict which zinc-carboxylate structure nucleates in networks containing mixed fatty-acid ligands and spatially varying crosslink density. Include kinetic trapping and subsequent transformations.
status: The 2021 work measured two-stage crystallization and strong effects of oil polymerization. A predictive map for mixed-ligand, heterogeneous paint remains a proposed extension.
why: Different soap populations produce different material responses.
key_works: J. Hermans, L. Zuidgeest, P. Iedema, S. Woutersen, and K. Keune (2021), “The kinetics of metal soap crystallization in oil polymers,” [DOI: 10.1039/D1CP03479K](https://doi.org/10.1039/D1CP03479K).

title: Acetic-acid generation versus delayed release in cellulose acetate
open: Infer current ester-hydrolysis rate and retained acetic-acid inventory separately from measured emissions. Distinguish new production from release of acid generated earlier.
status: A 2025 study of seven historical objects found thickness-dependent diffusion and evaporation regimes. Those emission measurements do not uniquely establish the internal acid-generation rate.
why: Prevents ventilation-induced emission changes from being misinterpreted as changes in polymer decay.
key_works: M. Novak et al. (2025), “A quantitative study of acetic acid emissions from historical cellulose acetate at room conditions,” [DOI: 10.1038/s40494-025-01551-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s40494-025-01551-y).

title: Ambient aluminium catalysis in alum-treated archaeological wood
open: Separate proton-catalyzed damage from aluminium-mediated catalysis at storage temperatures. Identify active aluminium species and quantify their contribution at matched acidity and moisture.
status: Oseberg conservation research and a 2021 collection comparison show that acidity alone does not explain observed damage patterns. Aluminium’s additional ambient catalytic contribution remains insufficiently quantified.
why: Neutralization may leave a degradation pathway active.
key_works: J. J. Łucejko et al. (2021), “Comparative chemical investigations of alum treated archaeological wood from various museum collections,” [publisher article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s40494-021-00517-0); S. Braovac et al. (2018), “Navigating conservation strategies: linking material research on alum-treated wood from the Oseberg collection to conservation decisions,” [DOI: 10.1186/s40494-018-0241-y](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40494-018-0241-y).

title: Carbon and electron sources of iron oxalate in gall-ink paper
open: Determine whether oxalate in aged gall-ink paper derives from cellulose, ink polyphenols, or another component. Identify the coupled electron donor for Fe(III) reduction.
status: A 2026 ink/mockup study observed ferrous oxalate emerging as ferric polyphenol complexes were depleted. Product detection did not establish its carbon source or complete redox balance.
why: Determines whether iron oxalate diagnoses paper destruction, ink alteration, or both.
key_works: M. Nunes et al. (2026), “From Ink to Mockup: An Integrated Study of Historical Gall Ink Formulations and Their Impact on Paper,” [DOI: 10.1002/cplu.202500369](https://doi.org/10.1002/cplu.202500369).

title: Cellulose molar-mass analysis in gum-rich inked rag paper
open: Recover the cellulose chain-length distribution from microsamples of historic rag paper containing iron-gall or logwood ink and gum arabic. Demonstrate unbiased recovery without preparation-induced depolymerization.
status: A 2025 study reported unsuccessful size-exclusion chromatography after tricarbanilation for historical rag paper and some inked samples. Incomplete derivatization or dissolution limited the measurements.
why: The failure excludes objects for which degradation measurements are particularly valuable.
key_works: K. Retko, L. Legan, J. Malešič, and P. Ropret (2025), “Exploring the properties and degradation of iron gall inks and logwood ink and their mixtures on various paper supports,” [DOI: 10.1038/s40494-025-01732-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s40494-025-01732-9).

title: Electron balance and binder-dependent branches of red-lead whitening
open: Identify the electron donor reducing Pb(IV) in Pb₃O₄ during natural whitening. Close carbon, chlorine, and lead balances along binder-dependent product branches.
status: A 2026 thirty-month exposure study detected alteration from twelve months onward, with different intermediates in egg-yolk and rabbit-glue paints before cerussite formation. Those phase sequences leave the full reaction balance unresolved.
why: Explains why binder choice changes the route and timing of pigment loss.
key_works: D. Jiménez-Desmond, J. S. Pozo-Antonio, and C. Cardell (2026), “Discolouration of historical pigments: Investigating the whitening of red lead tempera-based mock-ups after natural weathering,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.culher.2026.02.010](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.culher.2026.02.010).

title: Native structures of latent copper–sulfhydryl complexes in wine
open: Identify copper complexes storing releasable H₂S, including copper oxidation state, nuclearity, sulfide content, and glutathione coordination. Measure them before analytical reagents perturb their equilibria.
status: Allison and Sacks showed in 2021 that brine release depends on halide chemistry and glutathione. The assay defines a releasable pool without uniquely identifying its native molecular constituents.
why: Predicts whether copper treatment removes sulfur or temporarily conceals it.
key_works: R. B. Allison and G. L. Sacks (2021), “Brine-Releasable Hydrogen Sulfide in Wine: Mechanism of Release from Copper Complexes and Effects of Glutathione,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.jafc.1c04885](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jafc.1c04885).

title: Electron donors sustaining sulfide regeneration in anoxic wine
open: Identify constituents supplying electrons for Cu(II) reduction and conversion of sulfur at oxidation state −I into H₂S sulfur at −II. Balance oxidized organic products against regenerated volatile sulfur.
status: The 2024 remediation study explicitly identifies these electron donors as missing. Copper-treatment, filtration, and adjuvant experiments did not resolve the recurring-sulfide mechanism.
why: Exposes the driver of sulfur recurrence after oxygen depletion.
key_works: D. Sánchez-Gimeno, E. Vela, V. Ferreira, and I. Ontañón (2024), “Alternative strategies for eliminating hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol from wine: results and learnings,” [DOI: 10.20870/oeno-one.2024.58.4.7655](https://doi.org/10.20870/oeno-one.2024.58.4.7655).

title: Non-methionine methanethiol precursors in aged wine
open: Identify the precursor pool sustaining methanethiol production when measured free-methionine depletion cannot account for release. Determine sulfur yields and temperature-dependent conversion kinetics.
status: A 2025 study followed twelve wines for up to eighteen months at 35 °C and shorter periods at higher temperatures. Methanethiol production persisted without closure of the measured precursor balance.
why: Enables prevention of delayed sulfur faults missed by initial volatile measurements.
key_works: S. Ainsa-Zazurca, I. Ontañón, and V. Ferreira (2025), “Kinetic Studies on the Ability of Wines to Produce Hydrogen Sulfide (H2S) and Methanethiol (MeSH),” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.jafc.5c04010](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jafc.5c04010).

title: Chemically specified can-liner acceptance tests for sulfited beverages
open: Establish qualification tests connecting verified polymer chemistry, coating continuity, and beverage-contact reactivity to H₂S formation across production lots. Predict shelf life and detect consequential material substitutions.
status: Cornell researchers documented a 2025 industrial case in which generic terminology permitted an acrylic-liner substitution associated with roughly tenfold greater H₂S in accelerated testing. Labels such as BPA-NI did not specify the necessary chemistry.
why: Addresses an observed procurement and quality-control failure.
key_works: G. Sacks, J. Goddard, A. Montgomery, H. Ramírez, and A. Abegunde (2025), “Wine or cider can liner terminology – precision matters!” [Cornell industrial research note](https://cals.cornell.edu/news/2025/06/wine-or-cider-can-liner-terminology-precision-matters).

title: Pathway-resolved sulfur balance for coffee 2-furfurylthiol loss
open: Quantify 2-furfurylthiol consumption through quinone addition, pyrazinium trapping, oxidation, and other sinks versus physical partitioning. Close the sulfur balance in brewed coffee.
status: A 2024 model study implicated hydroxyhydroquinone oxidation products and found 3.3% 2-furfurylthiol remaining after thirty minutes under its conditions. Earlier work established melanoidin-related trapping; native pathway contributions remain unresolved.
why: Distinguishes irreversible aroma destruction from reversible retention.
key_works: Z. Sun et al. (2024), “Influence of aroma binding factors of coffee matrix on characteristic aroma in a model system,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.lwt.2024.116930](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lwt.2024.116930); T. Hofmann and P. Schieberle (2002), “Chemical Interactions between Odor-Active Thiols and Melanoidins Involved in the Aroma Staling of Coffee Beverages,” [DOI: 10.1021/jf010823n](https://doi.org/10.1021/jf010823n).

title: IRC7-independent thiol release in brewing yeast
open: Identify enzymes and substrates responsible for aroma-thiol release retained after IRC7 deletion. Demonstrate necessity and sufficiency using genetic perturbation and enzyme reconstitution.
status: A 2025 comparison found an IRC7 knockout with thiol release resembling its parent. The result implicates alternative routes without identifying the compensating enzyme system.
why: Makes strain performance predictable when the commonly targeted β-lyase gene is insufficient.
key_works: R. Samia, A. Shayevitz, T. Fischborn, and T. H. Shellhammer (2025), “Wort Nitrogen and Yeast Strain Drive Thiol Release, Flavor Expression, and Fermentation Performance in Beer,” [DOI: 10.1080/03610470.2025.2530859](https://doi.org/10.1080/03610470.2025.2530859).

title: Post-fermentation formation of 3SH and 3S4MP in beer
open: Resolve why 3-sulfanylhexan-1-ol and 3-sulfanyl-4-methylpentan-1-ol continue increasing after primary fermentation. Separate enzymatic cleavage, abiotic formation, and release from inaccessible pools.
status: A study available online in July 2026 documented continued increases and gene-expression profiles that did not adequately explain thiol trajectories. The biochemical and physical contributions remain unresolved.
why: Enables control of maturation-stage aroma after primary fermentation slows.
key_works: R. S. Samia, C. Chenot, K. Divilov, A. Shayevitz, and T. H. Shellhammer (2026), “A time-course assessment of polyfunctional thiol release and yeast gene expression in dry-hopped beers,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.fochms.2026.100445](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fochms.2026.100445).

title: Structural verification of hydrolysis-resistant smoke-taint precursors
open: Authenticate structures and glycosidic linkages of precursor features persisting across microbial treatments. Establish standards that distinguish resistant glycosides from isomers, misassignments, and analytical artifacts.
status: The 2025 study reported 93 putatively assigned precursor features; 62 persisted across all ten tested yeast strains. Accurate-mass assignments alone do not establish structure or enzymatic resistance.
why: Enzyme discovery requires reliable identities for the resistant substrates.
key_works: H. Piao, T. S. Collins, and T. Henick-Kling (2025), “Investigation of smoke-taint precursor modification by glycosidase activity in diverse wine yeast and bacterial strains,” [DOI: 10.3389/fmicb.2025.1679638](https://doi.org/10.3389/fmicb.2025.1679638).

title: Chemical identity of sake fraction DMTS-P2
open: Identify the active constituent or constituents of DMTS-P2 and establish how they yield dimethyl trisulfide. Determine whether activity requires interacting compounds separated during purification.
status: The 2009 work identified DMTS-P1 but left another active fraction unresolved. Isogai’s thesis investigated DMTS-P2 and its interaction with a neutral fraction without converting those operational fractions into molecular structures.
why: Resolves a source of stale-sake sulfur aroma beyond the identified P1 pathway.
key_works: A. Isogai et al. (2009), “Screening and Identification of Precursor Compounds of Dimethyl Trisulfide (DMTS) in Japanese Sake,” [DOI: 10.1021/jf802582p](https://doi.org/10.1021/jf802582p); A. Isogai (2009), “清酒の熟成に関与する香気成分およびその生成機構に関する研究,” [doctoral thesis](https://ir.lib.hiroshima-u.ac.jp/31097/files/19891).

title: Grape-derived dimethyl-trisulfide precursors in wine
open: Identify grape-derived compounds required for substantial DMTS formation during aging. Establish their contribution independently of methanethiol and the sake precursor DMTS-P1.
status: The 2017 study found that dead yeast in synthetic must did not reproduce grape-juice behavior, while known precursors explained only a minor contribution. The operative grape-derived structures remained unidentified.
why: Connects grape and must composition to delayed sulfur defects.
key_works: N. Nishibori, A. Kuroda, O. Yamada, and N. Goto-Yamamoto (2017), “Factors Affecting Dimethyl Trisulfide Formation in Wine,” [DOI: 10.3136/fstr.23.241](https://doi.org/10.3136/fstr.23.241).

title: Chromophore responsible for Sauvignon-blanc pinking
open: Identify the chromophore responsible for the studied Sauvignon-blanc pinking and reproduce its behavior at native concentrations. Distinguish trace anthocyanins from alternative oxidized phenolic products.
status: Anthocyanins were established as a cause in Síria wines in 2014. The 2022 Sauvignon-blanc study remained inconclusive: its 1 mg/L detection limit exceeded the 0.3 mg/L visibility threshold reported for Síria.
why: Improves susceptibility testing and targeted prevention.
key_works: A. P. Nel, W. J. du Toit, and F. P. van Jaarsveld (2022), “Attempted Identification of Causal Constituents of Pink Discolouration in White Wines,” [DOI: 10.21548/43-1-4812](https://doi.org/10.21548/43-1-4812); J. Andrea-Silva et al. (2014), “Origin of the pinking phenomenon of white wines,” [DOI: 10.1021/jf500825h](https://doi.org/10.1021/jf500825h).

title: Unassigned species in the isolated oleocanthal–Tris adduct
open: Assign additional NMR resonances in isolated oleocanthal–Tris material. Determine whether they represent constitutional isomers, degradation products, or other species, and reconstruct the evolving mixture.
status: Major amine adducts were characterized in 2025, but additional A/B/C signals in the small Tris-adduct sample remained ambiguous. The target is this unresolved material specifically.
why: Buffer-generated products can change what an oleocanthal assay measures.
key_works: D. Di Risola et al. (2025), “Spontaneous Reaction of Oleacein and Oleocanthal with Primary Amines: A Biochemical Perspective,” [DOI: 10.3390/molecules30071645](https://doi.org/10.3390/molecules30071645).

title: Calibrated unstable-polysulfide standards for wine sulfur inventories
open: Produce calibrated reference materials for cysteine-, glutathione-, and mixed-ligand polysulfides containing three to five sulfur atoms. Quantify stability and analytical interconversion, including isotope-labeled standards.
status: A 2023 study isolated dicysteinyl pentasulfide while noting shortages of individual standards. A 2026 study measured matrix-dependent evolution; traceable calibration of the broader interconverting family remains a proposed data target.
why: Enables closure of reservoirs feeding delayed sulfide release.
key_works: S. Dekker et al. (2023), “Monitoring hydrogen sulfide de-novo formation from polysulfides present in wine using ion chromatography and ultra high-pressure liquid chromatography combined with fraction collection and high-resolution mass spectrometry,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.chroma.2023.463805](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chroma.2023.463805); Y. Hou et al. (2026), “Understanding polysulfide evolution in wine: insights from accelerated ageing and real-time cellaring in different packaging,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.fochx.2025.103447](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fochx.2025.103447).

title: Mechanical barrier lowering versus impact heating in solid-state Wittig chemistry
open: Quantify conversion attributable to force-dependent barrier modification versus transient local heating. Resolve the reacting contact beyond average jar-temperature measurements.
status: The 2026 single-ball experiments found nearly linear conversion versus cumulative energy but explicitly did not distinguish direct mechanical activation from microscopic thermal spikes.
why: Determines whether contact mechanics or heat dissipation should be changed to improve efficiency.
key_works: J. Templ and L. Borchardt (2026), “Experimental Isolation of Single Impact, Cumulative Energy, Aging, and Liquid-Assisted Grinding Effects in Mechanochemical Reactions,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.202523191](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202523191).

title: From measured mill-wall forces to energy deposited in reacting grains
open: Infer distributions of strain, temperature, and dissipated energy at active powder contacts from instrumented-mill measurements. Validate the inference as particle size, adhesion, and mechanics evolve.
status: Force-sensing jars and impact-energy measurements were demonstrated in 2025, including salt-powder and Knoevenagel tests. Transfer from boundary forces to the microscopic reacting environment remains a proposed multiscale target.
why: Supplies physical inputs for rate laws transferable between mills.
key_works: E. Nwoye, K. Floyd, J. Batteas, and J. Felts (2025), “Experimental quantification of impact force and energy for mechanical activation in vibratory ball mills,” [DOI: 10.1039/D5MR00059A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5MR00059A).

title: Predicting lactide stereoblock lengths during the first minute of milling
open: Predict PLLA/PDLA block-length distributions from competition between solid mixing and ring-opening polymerization. Test whether interrupted milling selects reproducible distributions before monomer domains homogenize.
status: A 2025 study observed homogenization within about one minute, early stereoblock formation, and more atactic material after prolonged processing. Quantitative sequence-distribution prediction remains a proposed next target.
why: Connects a processing variable to polymer microstructure and crystallization.
key_works: E. S. Go et al. (2025), “Insights into Mechanochemical Solid-State Ball-Milling Reaction: Monitoring Transition from Heterogeneous to Homogeneous Conditions,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacsau.5c00322](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacsau.5c00322).

title: Predicting sonochemical yield from bubble survival between ultrasound pulses
open: Predict radical production from bubble dissolution, coalescence, and reactivation during pulse-off intervals. Transfer predictions across dissolved gases and surfactant kinetics without refitting effective bubble populations.
status: The 2026 study at 337 kHz found that longer off-times reduced activity despite reduced coalescence, implicating dissolution under its conditions. Transfer to other bubble populations remains unresolved.
why: Enables pulse schedules improving chemical yield per acoustic energy.
key_works: M. C. Nolan, H. A. Fernandez, A. N. Cowen, F. R. Fuller, and L. K. Weavers (2026), “Bubble coalescence and dissolution effects on sonochemical activity in pulsed wave ultrasound systems,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.ultsonch.2026.107787](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ultsonch.2026.107787).

title: A location-resolved calibration connecting sonochemical dosimeters
open: Establish absolute calibration among iodide oxidation, fluorescent radical probes, sonoluminescence, and sonochemiluminescence. Separate reactive flux reaching bubble interiors, interfaces, and bulk liquid.
status: A 2025 comparison covered 114 conditions spanning 22–2,000 kHz. Optical and chemical readouts correlated differently, leaving a universal brightness-to-radical conversion unsupported.
why: Makes reactor comparisons meaningful across probes and geometries.
key_works: Y. Zhu, X. Zhu, X. Pan, L. X. Liu, and M. J. Bussemaker (2025), “Correlation of sonochemical activities measured via dosimetry and an area-selective analysis of sono(chemi)luminescence,” [DOI: 10.1039/D5MR00006H](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5MR00006H).

title: Predicting the power threshold for sonochemical quenching after scale-up
open: Predict when additional acoustic power reduces chemical productivity as geometry, gas content, and solutes change. Demonstrate control that maintains a productive bubble regime.
status: A 2025 study distinguished regimes involving wave interference, bubble growth, and a standing-to-traveling-wave transition. A transferable threshold across reactor geometries remains a proposed engineering target.
why: Prevents scale-up from consuming more power while generating fewer reactive species.
key_works: R. Aoki, K. D. Hattori, and T. Yamamoto (2025), “Revisit to the mechanism of quenching: Power effects for sonochemical reactions,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.ultsonch.2025.107419](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ultsonch.2025.107419).

title: Separating cavitation chemistry from contact electrification on sonicated PTFE
open: Close electron, radical, and product balances while distinguishing sonolysis, hydrophobic-interface cavitation, and contact electrification. Include evolving particle populations and polymer-derived products.
status: The 2025/2026 study reported enhanced chemical outputs with fine PTFE particles generated during sonication. Quantitative partitioning of the coupled mechanisms remains a proposed measurement target.
why: Establishes which material property controls enhancement and whether the solid remains catalytic.
key_works: H.-D. P. Nguyen et al. (2026; online 2025), “Highly Efficient Sono-Contact-Electrocatalysis Enabled by Fine-Scale and Ultrasonically Generated Polytetrafluoroethylene Particles,” [DOI: 10.1002/aesr.202500240](https://doi.org/10.1002/aesr.202500240).

title: Measuring nitrogen-oxide branching during cavitation collapse and quenching
open: Measure nitrogen-oxide intermediates and cooling histories responsible for nitrate/nitrite branching. Predict aqueous products from measured bubble conditions without an adjustable hidden peak temperature.
status: A 2026 study combined isotope evidence and modeling to support gas-phase activation during collapse and demonstrated noble-gas control of selectivity. Direct transient-to-product accounting remains a narrower experimental target.
why: Identifies limitations from nitrogen activation, cooling, and product survival.
key_works: X. Pan et al. (2026), “Mechanistic insights into the non-equilibrium thermodynamics of nitrogen fixation via acoustic cavitation,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-69466-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-69466-1).

title: Hydrogen-bond-defect control of water photoionization branching
open: Measure whether particular pre-existing hydrogen-bond defects select hydrogen-atom formation versus proton-coupled electron transfer. Obtain branching probabilities conditioned on initial local structure.
status: The 2026 simulations localize excitation at hydrogen-bond defects and predict competing ultrafast pathways. Experimental selection and observation of the implicated configurations remain a proposed mechanistic test.
why: Connects liquid-water structure to initial radiation and ultraviolet products.
key_works: G. Díaz Mirón et al. (2026), “Simulating the Photochemical Birth of the Hydrated Electron in Liquid Water,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-70045-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-70045-7).

title: Assigning the emitting ion–radical configurations formed by photoexcited water
open: Identify relative configurations of the hydrated electron, hydronium, and hydroxyl radical responsible for predicted transient visible emission. Test whether emission and recombination require the proposed water-mediated pairs.
status: The 2026 simulations predict picosecond-lived configurations influencing emission. Correlating a particular emitting structure with its chemical fate remains an experimental test.
why: Turns transient emission into a structural probe of early radiation chemistry.
key_works: G. Díaz Mirón et al. (2026), “Simulating the Photochemical Birth of the Hydrated Electron in Liquid Water,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-70045-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-70045-7).

title: Contact-pair separation versus valence trapping for hydrated uracil electrons
open: Determine rates and yields of solvent separation versus valence-bound uracil-anion formation as hydration approaches bulk conditions. Resolve the role of the first separating water molecule’s position.
status: The 2025 cluster study identified a mechanism in which one water molecule separates an electron–molecule contact pair and suppresses recombination. Quantitative transfer to larger fluctuating networks remains open.
why: Connects isolated-cluster capture to nucleobase chemistry in water.
key_works: C. J. Clarke, E. M. Burrow, and J. R. R. Verlet (2025), “The role of water molecules in the dissociation of an electron-molecule contact pair,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-57403-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-57403-7).

title: Direct isotope tests of room-temperature carbon tunneling in triplet ring closure
open: Test predicted tunneling contributions to room-temperature triplet-diradical closure in the housane and cagedione systems. Use position-specific carbon isotope effects and temperature-dependent branching to distinguish tunneling from spin-crossing changes.
status: The 2026 nonadiabatic instanton study examined four diradicals and predicted room-temperature tunneling dominance in two. Discriminating experiments at that temperature remain the validation target.
why: Establishes when heavy-atom quantum motion controls ordinary-temperature kinetics.
key_works: D. Mukherjee, K. D. Petryczkiewicz, and J. O. Richardson (2026), “Heavy-Atom Tunneling at Room Temperature Revealed by Instanton Theory,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.2372199](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.2372199).

title: Fluoride tunneling between two germanium centers of a molecular receptor
open: Realize the proposed double-germanium fluoride receptor and detect low-temperature intersite transfer with a tunneling signature. Distinguish exchange from static disorder and thermal hopping.
status: The ping-pong process was predicted in 2018. The 2025 experimental fluorine-tunneling paper still describes this receptor as hypothetical; its observed polyfluoride system is chemically distinct.
why: Tests deliberate geometric control of tunneling by a relatively heavy nucleus.
key_works: A. Nandi, A. Sucher, and S. Kozuch (2018), “Ping-Pong Tunneling Reactions: Can Fluoride Jump at Absolute Zero?” [DOI: 10.1002/chem.201802782](https://doi.org/10.1002/chem.201802782); C. Müller et al. (2025), “Experimental observation of quantum mechanical fluorine tunnelling,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-59008-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-59008-6).

title: Experimental verification of tunneling-driven XeF₆ pseudorotation
open: Separate quantum tunneling from residual thermal motion in low-temperature XeF₆ pseudorotation. Identify predicted splittings or isotope-sensitive exchange in a characterized environment.
status: Sedgi and Kozuch predicted rapid near-zero-temperature fluorine tunneling in 2020. The 2025 polyfluoride study still cites XeF₆ as a computational prediction.
why: Tests quantum dynamics in a classic fluxional hypervalent molecule.
key_works: I. Sedgi and S. Kozuch (2020), “Heavy atom tunnelling on XeF6 pseudorotation,” [DOI: 10.1039/D0CP03205K](https://doi.org/10.1039/D0CP03205K); C. Müller et al. (2025), “Experimental observation of quantum mechanical fluorine tunnelling,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-59008-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-59008-6).

title: Counterion survival of predicted IF₆⁻ and TeF₆²⁻ tunneling
open: Determine whether predicted low-barrier pseudorotation survives ion pairing and solid-state symmetry breaking. Establish when counterions suppress, split, or preserve fluorine tunneling.
status: The 2020 calculations predict faster tunneling for these isoelectronic ions than for XeF₆. Environment-dependent experimental realization remains a proposed extension of that species-specific prediction.
why: Tests whether heavy-atom tunneling persists in accessible ionic materials.
key_works: I. Sedgi and S. Kozuch (2020), “Heavy atom tunnelling on XeF6 pseudorotation,” [DOI: 10.1039/D0CP03205K](https://doi.org/10.1039/D0CP03205K).

title: Testing hyperconjugation as the cause of solvent-enhanced carbon tunneling
open: Test whether coordination-dependent geminal hyperconjugation explains tunneling-rate changes in the benzene oxide/oxepin system. Independently constrain coordination populations and distinguish barrier narrowing from energetic stabilization.
status: The 2025 calculations connect coordination motifs to C–C shortening and enhanced tunneling. Solvent-controlled tunneling already has experimental precedents; the open target is this proposed electronic cause and its quantitative prediction.
why: Could make solvent selection a rational control of heavy-atom tunneling.
key_works: C. J. Laconsay, I. Jain, T. Schleif, W. L. Karney, and J. I. Wu (2025), “Geminal hyperconjugation as a driving force for C–C bond shortening in heavy-atom tunnelling,” [DOI: 10.1039/D5SC02914G](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5SC02914G).

title: Ten-year novel desalination materials compatible with existing SWRO plants
open: Demonstrate a novel seawater-separation material or method combining potable-water production, improved energy and environmental performance, and a credibly projected operational lifetime of at least ten years. Provide a manufacturing and integration route to a 300,000 m³/day reference plant.
status: XPRIZE Water Scarcity began in 2024; Track B remained in competition in 2026. Its guidelines define this joint target and accelerated lifetime validation.
why: Connects molecular materials discovery to industrial separation hardware.
key_works: XPRIZE Foundation (2025), “XPRIZE Water Scarcity Competition Guidelines,” version 3.0, [competition and guidelines](https://www.xprize.org/competitions/water).
prize: Track B first prize: **US$8 million**; total Track B purse: **US$10.9 million**. These are competition awards subject to eligibility and judging; registration closed in 2025.

title: A validated weeks-to-decade lifetime test for novel desalination membranes
open: Establish an accelerated protocol predicting ten-year chemical and hydraulic degradation with quantified uncertainty. Show that acceleration preserves failure mechanisms under combined cleaning, fouling, oxidation, and compaction.
status: The 2025 guidelines explicitly identify the absence of a universal membrane-lifetime test and require protocols beyond their illustrative sequence. Validating the extrapolation remains distinct from passing individual short stress tests.
why: Makes lifetime claims comparable before procurement.
key_works: XPRIZE Foundation (2025), “XPRIZE Water Scarcity Competition Guidelines,” version 3.0, Appendix A.4, [competition and guidelines](https://www.xprize.org/competitions/water).
